> @michaelpj Another point that I should put into the text: not representing redeemers and datums as Data directly makes it harder for script authors, as they now have to know how their data object is encoded in order to actually work with it.

Well, that's only true if you consider people using Haskell & the PlutusTx framework for off-chain code which abstracts that away behind Template Haskell. Many developers have actually moved to other solutions, might it be Pluto, Plutarch, Helios, Aiken or Plu-ts, etc. And even more are actually using PlutusTx only for on-chain code, and use their own favorite stack for off-chain. In which case, there's a need to bridge the on-chain script interfaces with whatever off-chain solution people use. See for examples projects like Mesh or Lucid that are used for building transactions in TypeScript where it is needed to know how datums and redeemers are encoded in order to build transactions. 

Plus, irrespective of that, tools makers and builders are interested in knowing how the data object is encoded to inspect blockchain traffic and build better interfaces. This is what has motivated [CIP-0057](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/pull/258) to begin with. I don't think it's possible to completely hide the encoding format. If this was a initial desire then I can confidently say that it failed given the current situation. This is why I am insisting so much on documenting the interfaces. It is what enables the ecosystem to grow eventually.

Note that I don't think it is a bad situation because it impacts script authors very little. A script author will manipulate types using whatever framework/language they like. For example, they'll deal with Haskell data-types when using PlutusTx and they'll deal with Aiken data-types when using Aiken. Then, it doesn't changes the current status quo where those who use the Haskell Cardano / Plutus APIs down the line will benefits from existing framework functions to build and serialize transactions from Haskell types. While others who already need to manually construct datums and redeemers through their favorite off-chain language will continue doing so. With CIP-0057 we hope to standardize how we document this interface to possibly make this construction of datums and redeemers more automated. CIP-0085 doesn't change that; we'll simply need to extend the specification language from CIP-0057.

It has practical issues for us with Aiken (and I reckon other languages with a similar approach like Helios). Because we do not decode the script context, datums or redeemers. Aiken types are encoded as `Data` directly. So when one pulls a value of type `A` from the datum, and matches it with a value of type `A` in the script context, there's no conversion needed because both arguments have the same structural format. 

Now, if the script context is no longer a `Data` builtin type but a completely new term. That means we must either encode the script context as `Data` (likely no the preferred way because it can be quite large) or convert the datum / redeemer into terms (getting rid of the `Data` wrapper). 

Besides I really don't see any benefits in preserving `Data` on-chain, in the script evaluation. With the introduction of `constr`, any `Data` can be expressed as simpler terms, which means that an on-chain validator would be better off (performance wise) manipulating those less expensive terms directly instead of dealing with `Data`. 

`Data` is only truly useful on-chain if we need to have non-homogeneous data structures (like a array of _things_) like one might have in dynamically typed languages. I am not sure if I have any use case for it though to be frank but my brain is perhaps too used to strong static typing now. 

There's possibly a "security" argument in **not** translating a `Data` as an SOP. Because this translation would have to be done by the ledger, it means that there's no direct cost for it. When it's done as part of the script execution, then the cost of this translation is paid through the script execution. However, I'd argue that this cost is _implicitly_ covered by the standard fees. The larger the datum / redeemer, the larger the transaction and the higher the fees. So datums that are more computationally expensive to translate also comes with larger transaction fees. Thus, it doesn't introduce any new attack vectors in that sense. Plus, the cost of doing this translation is Haskell can probably be quantified and is in all likelihood negligible in front of e.g. a digital signature verification.

I think it's more a development process strategy here. First, make it work. Then, make it fast. Given the current implementation, it's relatively easy to add a translation from `Data` to `Term` and unless I am missing something, I believe that translation to be relatively trivial and _cheap_. So from a development perspective, it makes the change easy to implement and low-risk. 

Then, one can think in a second time how to make this more efficient by combining both steps and producing a `Term` directly when translating from ledger types.

The biggest current advantage of the Script Context being Data is cheap comparisons with arbitrary data structures in the script context using equalsData. 

A good example of this is called "output tagging". Which is based on doing a txref comparison to see which outputs contain a matching datum and thus are important to the executing script. ```suggestion
```suggestion
## Properties of Minimum Viable Governance (MVG)

This CIP aims to outline the specifications of Minimum Viable Governance (MVG) for Cardano. In this section the properties MVG must achieve are defined, the problems involved, and a a short introduction on the proposed solutions. 

+ [Initialization/bootstrap](#Initialization/bootstrap)
+ [No identity verification](#no-identity-verification)
+ [Minimize technical complexity](#minimize-technical-complexity)
+ [Distinct governance action classes](#distinct-governance-action-classes)
+ [Separation of hard-fork initiation from standard protocol parameter changes](#separation-of-hard-fork-initiation-from-standard-protocol-parameter-changes)
+ [Controlled number of active governance actions](#controlled-number-of-active-governance-actions)
+ [Legitimate governance actions](#legitimate-governance-actions)
+ [Ratification requirements table](#ratification-requirements-table)
+ [Insert property that using DReps achieves](#purpose-of-dreps)


### Initialization/bootstrap

**Property 1**: MVG must be able to initialize with a bootstrap mechanism for a blockchain lacking an MVG.

#### The botstrapping problem
As soon as we pull the trigger and enable this framework to become active on-chain, then without a constitutional committee, there would rapidly need to be sufficient DReps, so that the system did not rely solely on SPO votes. We cannot yet predict how active the community will be in registering as DReps, nor how reactive other Ada holders will be regarding delegation of votes.

#### Proposed solution
The constitutional committee comes into play to make sure that the system can transition from its current state into fully decentralized governance in due course.
Furthermore, in the long run, the committee can play a mentoring and advisory role in the governancedecisions by being a set of elected representatives who are put under the spotlight for their judgment and guidance in governance decisions.
Above all, the committee is required at all times to adhere to the Constitution and to ratify proposals in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution.

At first sight, the constitutional committee may appear to be a special committee that has been granted extra power over DReps.
However, because DReps can replace the constitutional committee at any time and DRep votes are also required to ratify every governance action,
the constitutional committee has no more (and may, in fact, have less) power than the DReps.

### No identity verification

**Property 2**: MVG omits Identity Verification.
Enforcing identity verification is very difficult without some centralized oracle, which we consider to be a step in the wrong direction.

#### Reducing the power of entities with large amounts of Ada

Various mechanisms, such as quadratic voting, have been proposed to guard against entities with a large amount of influence.
In a system based on "1 Lovelace, 1 vote", however, it is trivially easy to split stake into small amounts and undo the protections.
Without an on-chain identity verification system we cannot adopt any such measures.

#### Identity of DReps

We hope that the community will strongly consider only voting for and delegating to those DReps who provide something like a DID to identify themselves.
However, this CIP does not mention any kind of identity validation or verification for the members of the constitutional committee or the DReps.

### Minimize technical complexity

**Property 3**: MVG preferrably adds a limited amount of additional technical complexity to its blockchain protocol.

#### Piggybacking on stake pool stake distribution

The Cardano protocol is based on a Proof-of-Stake consensus mechanism, so using a stake-based governance approach is sensible.
However, there are many ways that could be used to define how to record the stake distribution between participants.
As a reminder, network addresses can currently contain two sets of credentials: one to identify who can unlock funds at an address
(a.k.a. payment credentials) and one that can be delegated to a stake pool (a.k.a. delegation credentials).

Rather than defining a third set of credentials, we instead propose to re-use the existing delegation credentials,
using a new on-chain certificate to determine the governance stake distribution. This implies that the set of DReps can (and likely will) differ from the set of SPOs,
so creating balance. On the flip side, it means that the governance stake distribution suffers from the same shortcomings as that for block production:
for example, wallet software providers must support multi-delegation schemes and must facilitate the partitioning of stake into sub-accounts should an Ada holder desire to delegate to multiple DReps,
or an Ada holder must manually split their holding if their wallet does not support this.

However, this choice also limits future implementation effort for wallet providers and minimizes the effort that is needed for end-users to participate in the governance protocol.
The latter is a sufficiently significant concern to justify the decision. By piggybacking on the existing structure,
the system remains familiar to users and reasonably easy to set up. This maximizes both the chance of success of, and the rate of participation in, the governance framework.

#### New Metadata structures

Both the governance actions and the votes use new metadata fields,
in the form of URLs and integrity hashes
(mirroring the metadata structure for stake pool registration).
The metadata is used to provide context.
For example, votes by the constitutional committee need an explanation as to why they are in line with
the constitution.
Governance actions need to explain why the action is needed,
what experts were consulted, etc.
Since transaction size constraints should not limit this explanatory data,
we use URLs instead.

This does, however, introduce new problems.
If a URL does not resolve, what should be the expectation for voting on that action?
Should we expect everyone to vote 'Abstain'?.
Is this an attack vector against the governance system?
In such a scenario, the hash pre-image could be communicated in other ways, but we should be
prepared for the situation.
Should there be a summary of the justification on chain?

**Alternative: Use of transaction metadata**

Instead of specific dedicated fields in the transaction format, we could instead use the existing transaction metadata field.

Governance-related metadata can be clearly identified by registering a CIP-10 metadata label.
Within that, the structure of the metadata can be determined by this CIP (exact format TBD), using an index to map the vote or governance action ID to the corresponding metadata URL and hash.

This avoids the need to add additional fields to the transaction body, at the risk of making it easier for submitters to ignore.
However, since the required metadata can be empty (or can point to a non-resolving URL),
it is already easy for submitters to not provide metadata, and so it is unclear whether this makes the situation worse.

Note that transaction metadata is never stored in the ledger state, so it would be up to clients to pair the metadata with the actions and votes in this alternative, and would not be available as a ledger state query.

### Distinct governance action classes

**Property 4**: MVG must separate classes of governance actions based on their overall impact to the blockchain protocol.

#### Problems

- Separation of Hard Fork Initiation from Standard Protocol Parameter Changes: 

In contrast to other protocol parameter updates, hard forks (or, more correctly, changes to the protocol's major version number) require much more attention.
Indeed, while other protocol parameter changes can be performed without significant software changes, a hard fork assumes that a super-majority of the network has upgraded the Cardano node to support the new set of features that are introduced by the upgrade.
This means that the timing of a hard fork event must be communicated well ahead of time to all Cardano users, and requires coordination between stake pool operators, wallet providers, DApp developers, and the node release team.

Hence, this proposal, unlike the Shelley scheme, promotes hard fork initiations as a standalone governance action, distinct from protocol parameter updates.

#### Solution ideas

- Ratification Requirements Table:

The requirements in the [ratification requirement table](#requirements) are explained here.
Most of the governance actions have the same kind of requirements:
the constitutional committee must reach quorum and the DReps must reach a sufficient number of
'Yes' votes.
This includes these actions:
* New committee/quorum (normal state)
* Update to the Constitution
* Protocol parameter changes
* Treasury withdrawal

- Motion of no-confidence:

A motion of no-confidence represents a lack of confidence by the Cardano community in the current constitutional committee, and hence the constitutional committee should not be included in this type of governance action.
In this situation, the SPOs and the DReps are left to represent the will of the community.

- New committee/quorum (state of no-confidence):

Similar to the motion of no-confidence, electing a constitutional committee
depends on both the SPOs and the DReps to represent the will of the community.

- The versatility of the info governance action:

While not binding on chain, the Info governance action could be useful in an number of
situations.  These include: ratifying a CIP, deciding on the genesis file for a new ledger era, recording initial feedback for future governance actions

- Hard-Fork initiation:

Regardless of any governance mechanism, SPO participation is needed for any hard fork since they must upgrade their node software.
For this reason, we make their cooperation explicit in the hard fork initiation governance action, by always requiring their vote.
The constitutional committee also votes, signaling the constitutionality of a hard fork.
The DReps also vote, to represent the will of every stake holder

### Controlled number of active governance actions

**Property 5**: MVG must be able to limit the number of active governance actions.

#### Problems

- Since governance actions are available for anyone to submit, we need some mechanism to prevent those individuals responsible for voting from becoming overwhelmed with a flood of proposals.

#### Solution ideas
- A large deposit is one such mechanism, but this comes at the unfortunate cost of being a barrier for some people to submit an action.
- Note, however, that crowd-sourcing with a Plutus script is always an option to gather the deposit.
- We could, alternatively, accept the possibility of a large number of actions active at any given time, and instead depend on off-chain socialization to guide voters' attention to those that merit it. In this scenario, the constitutional committee might choose to only consider proposals which have already garnered enough votes from the DReps.


### Legitimate governance actions

**Property 6**: MVG must guarantee the legitimacy of passed governance actions. Legitimacy can be loosely understood as having enough participation for a governance action to pass.

#### Problems
- Remove the possibility that, for example, 9 out of 10 Lovelace could decide the fate of millions of entities on Cardano.
- Losing participation over time
- MVG must already be bootstrapped, see the sections on bootstrapping.

#### Solution ideas
- An earlier draft of this CIP included the notion of an "active voting stake threshold", or AVST. One problem with the AVST is that it gives an incentive for SPOs to desire a low voting registration (since their votes then hold more weight). This is absolutely not a slight on the existing SPOs, but an issue with bad incentives.
- We solve the long-term participation problem by not allowing reward withdrawals (after the bootstrap phase) unless the stake is delegated to a DRep (including the two special cases, namely 'Abstain' and 'No confidence').

### Purpose of the DReps

**Property 7**: *TODO Define a property that DReps achieve*

#### Problem

*TODO: outline the issues if this property is ignored*

#### Solution ideas
- Use SPOs as DReps:  SPOs are chosen purely for block production and not all SPOs will want to become DReps. Voters can choose to delegate their vote to DReps without needing to consider whether they are also a good block producer, and SPOs can choose to represent Ada holders or not.
- New set of DReps: Nothing in this proposal limits SPOs from becoming DReps.
```

```suggestion
7. This system cannot rely on a trusted third party.

Additionally, here is a more opinionated (and potentially controversial) list of potential considerations for a CIP, presented purely to foster discussion:

1. There is currently no known decentralized "proof of personhood" system that is well specified and easily implementable, and without such a system, "one lovelace one vote" systems are the most effective defense against sybil attacks.
2. This system is highly dependent on the off chain user experience and community tooling, since very few users are reading raw CBOR dumps from the chain.
3. This system should be cognizant of the fact that different decisions can have different impact and risk thresholds.
4. This system cannot avoid the fact that stake pool operators of the network, collectively, always maintain control over a "pocket nuke": under sufficient discontent and misalignment with the will of governance, they can modify the code and initiate an uncontrolled hard fork to produce a separate chain aligned with their values.
5. Given the current near total control over these decisions that these founding powers have, any dilution of power that doesn't compromise the security of the chain or risk a deadlock is a worthwhile step to take.
```

If you want to reference the datum in another SC then yes, it does need to be maintained on-chain. I misunderstood that goal. However, that doesn't change my conclusion. Currently, CIP0025 recommends attaching metadata to the same transaction where the token forge occurs. This means that the metadata can only ever be associated with that token. To update the information, you just mint the token again with new metadata attached to the transaction. The downsides to this approach are:
1. The metadata format cannot be enforced.
2. If the information is needed for another SC, it isn't available since it is in the metadata.

Using an inline datum with a beacon token solves both of these issues. IMO The concern of having to maintain a datum for as long as necessary is not an issue:
1. Will it cause blockchain bloat? - No more so than using metadata since the information is identical between what would be in the datum and what would be in the metadata.
3. Will it cause a lot of locked ADA since UTxOs must have a minimum value? - The minimum value is probably only a few ADA (storing the beacon token with the inline datum in the UTxO) and this can be changed with protocol parameter changes. I don't think a few ADA is a big deal for registration. **This deposit is only necessary if the inline datum must be referenced in other SC exectutions.** If the datum does not need to be referenced, it can immediately be consumed (and beacon token burned) and the deposit can be recovered.

The benefits to this approach I think make up for having to use a deposit of a few ADA.  For this example, if the datums must be referenced by other SCs, all registration UTxOs could be locked at a specific SC address dedicated to registrations. The purpose of this SC is only to ensure the beacon tokens are burned whenever the datum is removed from the UTxO set. See [cardano-reference-scripts](https://github.com/fallen-icarus/cardano-reference-scripts) for an example. Since the datum is attached with the beacon, users can easily look up the UTxO TxIx and reference it in their own transactions, thus making the datum available during execution.

If the datum is never needed during SC executions, then there is no need to keep the inline datum on-chain. The last datum can always be found by looking at the last mint transaction for the native token and finding the output that had the beacon token. That output has the datum you are looking for. This is effectively the same as what CIP0025 currently suggests.

With this datum/beacon approach, the presence/absence of a beacon token absolutely conveys information about the datum. You can make it so that the beacon can only be minted if the beacon token is being stored with the proper datum (and at the proper address if needed) and the registering token is being minted in the transaction. As said before, if a datum is missing a required field, registration would automatically fail since the beacon token would fail to mint unless the datum format is followed. This means that if a UTxO is present with a datum but is missing the corresponding beacon token, then that registration is guaranteed to not be valid. Other smart contracts that use these datums can therefore look for the presence of the beacon token to ensure validity of the registration datum.

In short, using datums and beacon tokens does everything the metadata approach currently does but also guarantees the registration format is followed and allows other smart contracts to use the registration information in their executions. Using metadata labels and metadata cannot give you the same level of guarantees about the format nor can they allow other SCs to use them.

Edit:
As far as backwards compatibility goes for locked scripts, I don't think this approach would work as-is since you can't mint with the script anymore. A pubkey/script substitute would need to be used to signal "I am the creator".  However, going forward, I believe this approach is better for the reasons explained above.

Note that the pubkey/signature method is precisely what I am proposing specifically for the purpose of backwards compatibility and maintaining the ability to change things (like the project name or social media handles which are not necessarily part of the "what" of an NFT) even after the policy has locked.

I've actually renamed a reference in CIP-26 specific info to "Beacon/Reference Token" as I do think this method has merit but if the Beacon Token standard gains traction and popularity I would view them more as complementary to solve two different tasks rather than contrary or accomplishing the same.

The "Beacon Token" approach could be viewed as analogous to our original "Royalty Token" as proposed and co-authored by me back in 2021. i.e. mint a "nameless" token under the policy (native script) or contract (Plutus script) to provide a verifiable proof of ownership of the policy.

The only modification here is inserting the ability to use just the signing keys attached to the policy in order to make updates even past the timelock period of the script itself for non-mission-critical information (and of course the benefits to FT projects).

What about datum vs metadata? I do see these as accomplishing the same thing since the datum and metadata can carry the exact same information. You can convert this entire CIP (including the pubkey signature as ID) from using metadata to using datums and have the exact same functionality + enforcing the format and being able to reference the info in SC executions. Why would you still rather use metadata?

If the goal is not to maintain this information permanently via an inline datum (and most of the data is unnecessary for SC execution logic) then, as you say, they are basically two different, albeit with the same outcome, approaches to publish the data to the chain.

Monitoring the chain for a specific metadata key index and taking some downstream action is already trivial thanks to tools like [Oura](https://github.com/txpipe/oura). The (to be written) methodology for monitoring and validating these registrations will attempt to make use of as many currently existing, open source solutions as possible to minimize the hassle and burden on the part of third parties.

To your point, the goal of this top-level specification is not to inject data that is usable by smart contracts directly but to provide context to the scope (in this case tokens) within the purview of [CPS-0001](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/pull/371).

1. Publishing this data as transaction metadata versus an inline datum in a regular, simple transaction are equally error prone. The only solution, as far as I'm aware, would mean that a smart contract would need to be developed, deployed, and subsequently maintained (as new versions of this standard were developed over time) in order to **"force adherence to the format"**.
2. Utilizing a smart contract to force adherence to the data standard would break a large majority of the intentional flexibility designed into the standard as written. For example, a project may have CIP-25, CIP-27, CIP-60, and CIP-XX support or any combination of the above. All of which may have additional auxiliary data structures which may have one or more required or optional fields to provide additional information for off-chain purposes. I am going to reply to your comments out of order.

>  the query to find the same information when stored as an inline datum would be... Not nearly as user friendly

I believe this is false as long as the beacon token framework is used. I am not as familiar with db-sync itself to give you a specific query to execute however, I am familiar with both [Koios](https://www.koios.rest/) and [Blockfrost](https://blockfrost.dev/) that use db-sync as their backends. 

As an example, I will use Koios. The example assumes that you are using a registration beacon token that can only ever be minted in a registration transaction and the token name of the beacon token specifies what entity is being registered. You first use this [api](https://api.koios.rest/#get-/asset_history) to get the most recent mint transaction for that specific beacon token. From that response, you take the tx hash and use that in this [api](https://api.koios.rest/#post-/tx_utxos) to get all of the tx inputs and outputs. You only care about the outputs here. You filter the outputs for the UTxO that is holding the freshly minted beacon token in question. The inline datum attached to that UTxO is your registration data (it was returned as part of the previous response). From experience with my PoCs that do very similar things (using Blockfrost), the target inline datum is returned in about 1-2 seconds. I hardly think this counts as "user unfriendly". Based on my understanding of SQL, I see no reason why these two api queries + filtering can't be combined into one step which would make it even faster.

To your point about most of the information not being relevant for SC executions, I disagree again. When you create tools, it is impossible to know in advance how those tools will be used. Just because that information is useless to you does not mean it is useless to someone else. Using your NFT Project example, I think this *would* be useful in smart contract executions that deal with loyalty tokens. For example, the company of Discord can give a loyalty token to anyone who owns an NFT that is registered to use a valid discord server. You can trustlessly use a SC (created by Discord) for this where a user can try minting a loyalty token to themselves by referencing the UTxO with the NFT they own and the UTxO with that NFT's registration data. If the registration has a discord server registered, then the loyalty token can be minted to that user without any input from Discord the company. Discord can also make you provide a third input UTxO (owned by Discord the company) that has a datum of all valid discord servers currently registered to NFT projects to weed out fake servers; to mint a loyalty token, the server registered would also need to be in this third UTxOs datum.

As another example, one of the PoCs I am working on is an NFT marketplace where royalties are enforced by the Cardano settlement layer. There would literally be no way to avoid paying the royalties. Using beacon tokens and registration in datums, it would be possible for users to reference the royalty information for a given token when interacting with the marketplace. My current design is effectively doing this. This would allow the royalty information to be updated without needing to change the marketplace. Also, when a new version of the marketplace is introduced, creators can say in their royalty information which versions of the marketplace they consent to using. Users owning the NFT would only be allowed to use the versions in the royalty information. **This is all only possible if the royalty information is in a datum.**

To your point about flexibility, the design I have in mind is modular. There would be one beacon token for each registration form. If there are multiple tiers to a registration, then each tier would also have their own beacon token. This means users can choose which information to register and can register for multiple CIPs in one tx. Also, CIPs can be updated independently without impacting the other forms. Also the user can choose whether to leave this information on-chain for use in SCs. The user can always immediately consume the UTxO if they wish and the information would still be accessible to everyone else for off-chain use.

To your point about smart contract maintenance and deployment, there really isn't much maintenance since changing any of the code would result in an entirely new beacon token. What I am suggesting here is for CIPs that deal with registrations with datums to also provide a smart contract for everyone to use. If a bug is discovered, the smart contract that is stored with the CIP can be updated very quickly. Changes are made to current CIPs fairly frequently. Whenever a new version of a form is proposed, that proposal must also include the new smart contract for people to use. BTW, these smart contracts are pretty small in size. From my experience with the PoCs, they are only about 100 lines of code.

> I am actively working on increasing the future flexibility of this specification to support additional contexts such as stake pools, addresses, and more.

Since the beacon tokens are modular, new specifications can easily be added with this approach too. The limit for the number of registrations that can be made in a single transaction is likely at least 10. This seems like more than enough for now. This limit will grow as Cardano's tx limits grow.

In the case of optional fields, this is actually easy to do with datums thanks to the `Maybe` Haskell type (or `Optional` type in other languages). If the field isn't required, it is okay to leave it blank. It would basically just appear as null in the JSON.

Finally, in regards to whether or not this is part of the scope of this CIP, again I stress that it is. Until now (with the beacon token framework) it was not simple enough to store registration information in a datum. But now it is which means, going forward, the community needs to actively discuss the pros and cons of using a datum instead of transaction metadata. The community can now decide if the trade-off profile of one is better suited for a given task than the other. However, since you have explicitly mentioned metadata everywhere in your CIP, you have implicitly taken a stand without explaining why in your CIP. If you actually want this discussion to be out-of-scope for your CIP (which is fine if you do) then you need to change it to be agnostic to whether the information is stored in a datum or metadata.

To be fair, as said before, being able to use datums is new. I apologize if you feel like I am singling you out given that all the other registration CIPs solidly deal with metadata. We all want what is best for Cardano and I am trying to spread the word about the possibility of using datums now. AFAICT, this discussion is the very first time anyone in the community has even remotely considered the idea. IMO, all previous CIPs should now be revisited with this datum vs metadata debate as well. Going forward, since there are now two different ways of doing the same thing, it is up to CIP authors to explain why they have chosen the option they chose.

I believe that we can eliminate both the refs and p definitions within individual token metadata here if we switch to a URI-schema to signal support by way of CIP-88. More details to be shown below.

I think the best way to embed references in existing metadata structures would be via a structured URI format as defined in the spec. Rather than just using a name and forcing all parsers to scan for references a defined URI schema would make it easier to detect.

**URI Format**
```cbor
uriSchema = {
  scheme : string .size (4..64) ; Examples: ar://, ipfs://, etc
  path * : string .size (1..64) ; Examples: [ar/ipfs hash]
}
```

**Hypothetical CIP-48 URI format**:

```cbor
uriSchema = ["cip48://","referenceA"]
```

In this way a downstream parser may quickly and easily identify a CIP-48-specific reference only on fields that match the format.

I'm sure this has been mentioned in one of the comments, but recently I have been thinking about the DRep system. Overall I think it makes sense in a liquid democracy model to be able to delegate your voting rights to an expert of your choosing, especially if you believe that you do not have enough time to review most or all governance actions thoroughly and instead delegate that responsibility. The argument I sometimes saw of "but it takes almost the same amount of time to review what your DReps are doing, you could just vote yourself" is valid. It will also take some time and effort to review your DRep (hopefully, this becomes easier with the right tools), but it's still less time-consuming than reading through each GA. What seems most realistic to me is that most ada holders will just set their delegation once and leave it as that. They won't monitor their DRep as long as no controversial decision is being voted on that affects them, and even then, most won't take any action. This is scary. That means that DReps will do all they can to amass delegations from the Cardano community to boost their decision-making power, think about SPO shilling, but on a whole different level. As no specific parameters are set for the maximum amount of ada a DRep can control, we could see only a handful of DReps ending up on top that decide that fate of us all. A system must be designed to avoid centralization of power, or else, even with the best intentions, it will eventually happen. Look at bitcoin mining and the centralization of hash rate power or the US's current political two-party system. 

So what can we do?
The most straightforward answer to just set a max ada amount per DRep sounds good initially, but this would also mean the idea of the pre-defined DReps has to be tossed, as the rules also apply to them. The question is also, what is the right amount of max ada for this parameter? This way still wouldn't block existing DReps from registering a new DRep certificate, like nobody stops the stake pool operator from opening a new pool. Not my preferred choice.

I'd instead like to see a parameter protocol defining the number of epochs that the DRep delegation certificate is valid. This would require the delegator to renew their vote delegation certificate actively. I was thinking about something similar to KES as the block-producing nodes use, or something similar that would allow the delegators to renew their certificate. That means if a delegator doesn't renew their vote delegation certificate, their stake is not counted as an active voting stake. 

Introducing this parameter of a maximum duration for a valid vote delegation certificate would mitigate the risk of "set and forget" voting delegations. It would leave some responsibility of the governance process with the voters, which should be one of the core duties each Cardano citizen must comply with if they want to participate in governance. As currently proposed, a one-time delegation to a DReps doesn't cut it.

Liquid democracy systems often allow transitive delegation, where your delegate can themselves delegate their vote further. This can partially mitigate the issue, because an end-user can delegate instead to someone who they trust to _pick a good final delegate_ rather than to someone they trust to _vote the way they want_. This creates some virtuous division of labour: you have some people (final delegates) who focus on scrutinizing proposals, and some people (intermediary delegates) who focus on scrutinizing final delegates. More generally, you can always delegate by picking someone you _do_ trust and who is _more_ informed than you are.

The levels of certification, as mentioned in the paragraph, are defined based on the type of certification issuer and the level of testing and verification involved.

Level 1 certification is provided by testing laboratories, which typically involve automated and manual testing to ensure the DApp/project (mainly their smart contract) meets certain functional and security requirements.

Level 2 certification is provided by Cardano's auditors, who perform a more detailed review of the DApp's/project's code, architecture, and security, to ensure that it meets higher standards.

Level 3 certification is provided by Cardano certification issuers and verification services, which typically involve a more comprehensive review of the DApp's/project's design, implementation, and security, and may include formal verification methods to mathematically prove the correctness of the DApp's/project's behavior.

In terms of the differences between auditors and verifiers, auditors typically focus on reviewing the code and implementation of the DApp/project, while verifiers may also take into account the overall design and architecture of the DApp/project. Additionally, verification may involve formal methods such as model checking, theorem proving or static analysis are commonly used in verification to rigorously verify the correctness of a DApp's/project's behavior. For example, model checking involves systematically exploring all possible states of a DApp/project to check if it satisfies certain properties, while theorem proving involves using mathematical logic to prove that a DApp/project behaves correctly under all possible circumstances. These formal methods are typically not used in auditing, which may rely more on manual review and testing.

Can we please be _much_ more explicit about what we do with the VRF.

A VRF is not a digital signature scheme, it's a verifiable random function. So please don't refer to VRF signatures. There's no such thing. There is a VRF _proof_. And the VRF needs an input. Lets be explicit about what the input is.

I believe it is essential to implement the proposed changes, as they appear to be reasonable and beneficial. In particular, I would like to emphasize the importance of requiring a unanimous "yes" vote from all currently active CC members when altering the quorum size. This is crucial for several reasons:

1. **Ensuring Consensus:** A unanimous vote guarantees that all committee members are in agreement, fostering a collective decision-making process that encourages collaboration and harmony within the group.
2. **Upholding Integrity:** By requiring the approval of all active members, it becomes more difficult for a minority to manipulate or unduly influence the decision-making process. This helps maintain the integrity and fairness of the committee's actions.
3. **Mitigating Potential Conflicts:** Unanimous agreement on such a critical matter minimizes the potential for conflicts or disagreements arising from differing opinions or perspectives. This ultimately leads to a more cohesive and effective committee.

I am uncertain if the MVG model allows for a unanimous voting requirement when altering the quorum size. However, I believe it is vital to explore this possibility to ensure that important decisions, such as adjusting the quorum threshold, are made by all active CC members in unison.

I think this has been pasted in verbatim from a Slack conversation, and it sounds a bit informal. In addition it mentions "this tool" and I'm not sure  what that was now.  I suggest rewriting this as follows.

----

It's clear from these figures that the limiting factor is the script size: about 300 G1 points or 150 G2 points can be processed in a single script before exceeding the script size limit, but the maximum CPU usage is only 55% of the the maximum CPU budget.  If the serialisation (involving both x- and y-coordinates) was used instead then there would be some saving in execution time, but a single script would only be able to process about half as many points and it's unlikely that the time savings would compensate for that.  For example, uncompressing 50 G2 points would cost about 1,655,000,000 CPU ExUnits and deserialising them would cost about 54,788,000, which is 1,600,000,000 ExUnits cheaper. At the time of writing, this equates to 0.27 Ada.  However, 50 serialised G2 points take up 4800 more bytes than 50 compressed ones, and the extra bytes would cost 0.36 Ada.  Thuis using serialisation would cost 0.09 Ada more than using compression for the same number of points.

In summary: even though uncompression is a lot more expensive per point than deserialisation, the size savings due to compression actually outweigh the speed gains due to serialisation because bytes per script are a lot more expensive than ExUnits per script in real terms.  For this reason, we propose to support the compressed format and only the compressed format.

If it helps, I can propose a well-scoped use case that can be a baseline test. 

The TLDR is to post verifiable messages signed from the EVM world to Cardano. The go-to signature scheme over there is `ecdsa-secp256k1` which signs on fixed-size messages. It's then natural to sign on message hash to support arbitrary message size, and the go-to hash function over there is `keccak256`. 
1. With `keccak256` in Plutus, a minting policy issuing authentic tokens can hash the posted message (to an output datum) with `keccak256` then verify it against the signature posted in redeemer on-chain.
2. Without it, the minting policy would have to trust the messenger, or force EVM agents to sign on `blake2b` hashes or sign with `ed25519`, etc.

We're asking signers to sign on both `keccak256` and `blake2b` message hashes at the moment for our project, but that wouldn't scale to a larger EVM ecosystem. Adding `keccak256` to Plutus, on the other hand, would open many doors for future integrations, like as @serejke outlined with Hyperlane.

I'm more than happy to work on this test case if accepted. We already have it written in Helios.

The URI spec _only_ has a `//` when the `authority` field is present; this [from the Wiki page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_Resource_Identifier#Syntax) (which is quoting the RFC) & itself an ABNF grammar... either the `//` _and_ the `authority` or present together or neither of them are present, so `//` is definitely _not_ a requirement for all URIs:

```
URI = scheme ":" ["//" authority] path ["?" query] ["#" fragment]
```
To disambiguate your middle question: for _our_ URI spec, `web+cardano:` always has to be present but `//` does not.

We are locked into supporting the payment links without an `authority` because for a long time that was the only implementation of these URIs that was getting professional consideration (someone suggested stake pool links in 2018 but nobody ever moved on it; timeline & links are in the PRs at the Discussion links).

As far as I know Yoroi in particular has supported payment links with only a path-query string that whole time: about 5 years now.  If I had to tell them they needed to commit to honouring an authority prefix (let's call it `//payment`) I would therefore expect about 5 years to get a response.

For some of the reasons in https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/pull/559#discussion_r1272675176, I'd be open to a new CIP with a `//payment` schema supporting a more developed syntax, but in the meantime those 2 interpretations (payment vs. `authority`) of everything after the `:`  can never collide: because one never has `//` and the others always do.

The "hope" that a payment address is valid would have been considered by editors when this CIP was originally debated from original authors @SebastienGllmt and @v-almonacid for that part of the scheme.  I believe it's not in the CIP because it's not the URI's "job"... how a wallet or perhaps a dApp would handle a URI with an invalid payment address would be up to the designers.

One application for a further `//payment` protocol (with a separate CIP) might be to use higher-level addresses e.g. AdaHandles.  In fact it could create a beautiful range of possibility (e.g. multiple and/or proportional payments): all of which are beyond the scope of this CIP which is basically becoming a `switch` to get to newly defined protocols for everything not considered 3 to 5 years ago.

That is at least an indicator that a hybrid URI-to-JSON stake portfolio protocol would be unpopular.  In fact, over 2 years after those discussions, CIP-0017 remains unimplemented as far as I know

I agree with this notion to some degree. There are lots of perfectly valid use cases for changing royalties. The key word here is **recommended**. With this distinction we allow for such use cases, as well as accommodating existing protocols such as Nebula which store the royalty in wallets rather than script addresses.

However, I believe the recommendation against _arbitrary_ royalty control is important. A collection whose fees are controlled arbitrarily can be easily sabotaged at the whim of the creator by increasing the royalties beyond a reasonable amount. This is bad assurance for buyers, and we should set the precedent for better schemes - the simplest of which is an always-fails validator.

We have implemented this in Grabbit, but haven't benchmarked it very thoroughly yet. I can get back to you on CPU, memory, etc. on the client side. 

As far as TX fees go, this shouldn't have much of an impact. Reading the fee is as simple as parsing the datum, which doesn't require consuming it at all.

One valid concern is the memory cost to the blockchain itself. This is definitely something worth thinking about, and the design has carefully considered memory usage to be as minimal as possible. I personally think the ability for validators to read the royalties directly & trustlessly is worth the cost many times over.

```hs
data Credential (kr :: KeyRole) c
  = ScriptHashObj !(ScriptHash c)
  | KeyHashObj !(KeyHash kr c)
  deriving (Show, Eq, Generic, NFData, Ord)
  
data ConwayGovCert c
  = ConwayRegDRep !(Credential 'DRepRole c) !Coin !(StrictMaybe (Anchor c))
  | ConwayUnRegDRep !(Credential 'DRepRole c) !Coin
  | ConwayUpdateDRep !(Credential 'DRepRole c) !(StrictMaybe (Anchor c))
  | ConwayAuthCommitteeHotKey !(Credential 'ColdCommitteeRole c) !(Credential 'HotCommitteeRole c)
  | ConwayResignCommitteeColdKey !(Credential 'ColdCommitteeRole c) !(StrictMaybe (Anchor c))
```

Commented later, but: you have to have either the name or the id of the constructor, otherwise you can't distinguish two constructors with the same fields. And the whole point of this proposal is to not set the ids, so it has to be names.

If anything this proposal seems vanishingly unlikely to generate tags that are small? We're taking the result mod 2^32, so I'd expect to probably get uniform numbers over that range, which are going to be _way_ higher than 2^7.

More generally, since this proposal wants global ids, there can only be *7* types _globally_ that get the small ids. So I think this will definitely perform worse on space, but that might not matter.
I think it's the uniqueness that rules out the Haskell approach, not determinism.

There is nothing that necessitates any particular interpretation of the integers in a `Constr`. We have generally assumed they will be indices: in particular, favouring small numbers is a reflection of that (also see https://www.ietf.org/id/draft-bormann-cbor-notable-tags-09.html#name-enumerated-alternative-data).

The point about conversion to SOPs is a good one. If we are able to offer a fast conversion from `Data` to SOPs, then you really will want to use indices rather than arbitrary ids (since if you want to case analyze the constructor with tag n, you need to provide alternatives for all of the n-1 previous tags too!).

> What is the rationale behind relying on transaction witnesses rather than what was originally proposed?

After evaluating the situation, my colleagues and I found it puzzling to require two signatures 🤷. I reached out to @matiwinnetou for clarification and discovered the additional signature was initially implemented because Blockfrost did not support witness signatures in transaction fetching a year ago. However, I personally believe that our decision should not be solely based on whether Blockfrost supports a feature or not. With tools like cardano-cli, cardano-wallet, Daedalus, and cardano-services that do support witness signatures, it seems more logical and efficient to make this CIP simpler by adhering to this available technology.

> Just adds an extra step to the verification whilst also restricting the type of keys/crypto that can be used.

Indeed, our goal is to streamline the process. By focusing on simplification, we can avoid unnecessary steps in verification and avoid limiting the types of keys/crypto that can be used.

> I also liked the property that the one registering did not have to be the one creating and submitting the Tx.

While this flexibility might seem advantageous, I view the requirement for the same key used in initial dApp registration for updates (such as domain changes or rebranding) as a beneficial feature. It adds a layer of security and consistency, ensuring that only authorized updates are made to a dApp.

No, it's a privacy problem, because the 3rd party software gets all my data. They have my addresses (even for an enterprise account with "not bunchable" addresses because of lack of a stake part). They have my UTxO set. Doesn't matter if I use a new address for every new transaction, they have it all. They can track everything they want then. And I can't control it with the CIP30. I can't prevent it. And I can't hide it then, but they can share it to everyone. So it's almost the same as if I had posted my public keys on Twitter.

In a perfect world everything is perfect. But as a software engineer I can say that in a real world we have to deal with imperfect software which can work in imperfect way. With each new link in the chain of responsibility, new potential points of failure arise. Each new link increases the number of potential attack vectors if there is lack of checking. The goal of this CIP is to make all operations for the wallet as **explicit as possible**. The wallet won't have to recheck every field of the transaction passed to it from the outside, if it assembled the transaction itself and processed every aspect of it 100%.

In this case, even in an imperfect world, we will reduce the likelihood of problems.

As a wallet developer, I can say that user safety and protecting their interests is **the main concern**. > identifying addresses containing the first payment credential

This method of identification could incorrectly identify some stake credentials as belonging to the account of the first payment credential. Bob could create a mangled address with his own stake credentials and Alice's first payment credential. Bob could use this to make it appear that Alice has chosen to delegate some stake to a pool. 

Of course Alice, controlling the payment credential, could move control of the delegation to a different stake credential, but perhaps Alice isn't aware that this has happened or is inactive but staking her held ADA. Wallet software should only discover derived stake keys through discovery.

I didn't call it sequential discovery because according to this standard, the derivation does not need to be sequential, so sequential discovery could result in a subset of all derived keys.

thanks for the feedback @Ryun1, as you mentioned in your comment, DRep vote delegation and Stake delegation use the same key, so the two systems are intertwined at the protocol level, the only important consideration this CIP adds regarding DReps is that users will use more than one stake key and can have funds distributes among those stake keys, this will mean that users must also delegate their vote to the DReps for each key, for example:

Alice have a portfolio delegating to three pools, A, B and C with the following distribution 10%, 50%, 40%. She can chose to either delegate all three stake keys to the same DRep (effectively delegating 100% of her voting power to him) or delegate her different stake keys to different DReps, for example if she want to distribute her voting power between two DReps, she could delegate the same stake key used for pool A and B to DRep1 and the remaining stake key to DRep2 delegating to each each (approximately) 50% of her voting power, alternatively she could delegate to three different DReps. This is how the system works at the protocol level, the difference here is that wallets that implement this CIP will have the additionally flexibility to allow Alice to delegate to more than one DRep if she has more than one stake key.

As for how this would work with future types of delegations is hard to say since it will depend on the mechanics of those, but this CIP is not proposing/altering any feature at the protocol level, having multiple stake keys is already supported by the protocol, so I would assume there will be no conflict with any future use of stake keys unless there is a breaking protocol change in that regard.

one justification: because there is one convergent definition of HTML while the "industry standard" of Markdown has produced a bunch of flavours with irreconcilable special features.  Those special features in Markdown come from special symbol behaviour, while HTML is always delineated with tag symbols which can be specifically whitelisted herein.

The reason I'd argue for GHMD over html, is that it's a lot easier for someone (especially non-technical users) to *write* in a textbox, and it's also a lot less confusing to read if you're looking at the raw data without the formatting applied. If we do decide to resolve information for ScriptPurpose, then we should make the information we resolve consistent across all the different constructors. I think `ScriptHash` is a good option in that case, since it is universally useful across the common script types (Minting, Spending, Staking). 

But I really like the idea of integer indices for everything because then we can move towards a future where we can better take advantage of the unique efficiency benefits offered to us by transaction determinism that other smart contract platforms (ie EVM) cannot have access to (especially if in the far future we have support for constant access indexed data structures directly in the script context). I feel like currently, we haven't even begun to scratch the surface of utilizing the advantages afforded to us via Cardano's transaction determinism. 

For instance, since we know at the time of transaction construction what the majority of the script context will look like, we can theoretically bring most lookups from O(n) to O(1). Especially with [TxOut Redeemers](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/pull/735) you can imagine a world where common lookup operations like `findOwnInput`, `valueOf`, `findStateThreadOutput`, are all O(1). Instead of looking up elements on-chain, we look them up off-chain and then we pass the index into the on-chain computation which then only has to check that the element at that index is indeed what we claim it is.

I'm fine with any relaxing of these rules; This part was written when I was unsure whether even the most gentle version of this was going to be accepted.

When I've raised this in the past, the response I got was that any hiding of information about the transaction when constructing the script context was considered dangerous and wouldn't be supported.

Hence, my original proposal was about including reference scripts in the witness set, which isn't directly visible to the script context.

It was quite a pleasant surprise when MPJ suggested that we just allow reference inputs like normal and leave them off the script context.

Including this information in the witness set might be an attack vector.

The user signs the transaction body, not the witness set.

That means that once transaction is signed the witness set might still change, and the signature would be correct.

That implies the user agreed to sign something that is later modified.

This is not a problem for redeemers because usually the information present on redeemers is validated in the contract, so if an attacker modifies it, a carefully designed contract will fail.

In the example use case of the "`TxOutRef` in output datum" that information is indeed in the datum, which is part of the tx body, which is signed and hence immutable once signed (or else the signature is invalid).

if we move this info outside the body the `TxOutRef` can be modified after signing, leaving the contract vulnerable to double satisfaction.

In Python it is common to declare Sum Types / Unions after the declaration of the specific types i.e.

```python
class A

class B

class C

AB = Union[A, B]
ABC = Union[A, B, C]
```

In Haskell the definition of the Sum Types / Union at the same time declares the involved alternatives, hence all involved alternatives are known at the time of declaration (and known to be distinct)

```haskell
data AB = A | B
data ABC = A | B | C -- I guess this would throw an error for redeclaring the constructors A and B?
```

In case of collision during declaration of Sum Type, the compiler has to deny compilation and ask the user to manually declare a constructor id for the involved types. I think this is rare enough to have practically no impact on computation. Regarding attacks I don't think this schema is more vulnerable than any other schema. In the current Plutus schema constructor id overlaps are practically omnipresent (though never in any sum types that occur in the compiled contract)

Ah, I realised a complexity. The "linearized" order is not actually the order that makes checking the most straightforward. The reason is that value is specified on the _UTXI_. So when processing a transaction with a resolving output, you really want to have seen the corresponding UTXI already otherwise you don't know if it balances.

So the order for easiest transaction-by-transaction checking is one that satisfies the reverse condition: every UTXI comes before the output that resolves it.

Putting it another way, the _information_ flows in the opposite direction to the _value_.

I think this suggests that the zone should be ordered so that UTXIs come before their resolving outputs, and we keep the separate linearizability check. Alternatively, we could generate some extra state in the initial checking phase so we know about all the UTXIs up-front?

thanks @Thomas-Upfield - there are three parts to your proposition in (https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/pull/788#discussion_r1548249428), so I wanted to address all of them individually:
> a reminder for tooling providers, to remind them that when they display information from DRep metadata that they will be displaying user generated content.

👍 1) This is correct and sufficient: and also well-precented in the security field in considering information "tainted" whenever it is entered by a user.  Implementors, users, and potential regulators will be able to determine rights and responsibilities form this statement alone.

> And that for whatever reason, they may decide that they do not want to display certain user generated content to their other users.

👎 2) This is not necessary and leads immediately to the same red flags we pointed out at the meeting today: "condescension" I think we called it, and a suggestion of "nannying" that is considered obligatory according to one cultural bias but unacceptable in another.

If we suggest the censorship, it will be considered an _recommendation_ or at least an _endorsement_ of censorship, as well as an invitation to those potential regulators... so the "disclaimer" does not actually disclaim anything and will in fact be seen as an acceptance of liability that we wouldn't otherwise have.

> Therefore they may also need to introduce a TOS and some form of moderation to handle this.

👎 3) Also unnecessary for the same reason.  Making point 1) above is enough: to say that the tooling providers are posting and/or displaying user-sourced data.  They may "need" moderation and may not, and nobody can anticipate what their jurisdiction or legal precedent might be.  If "we" tell them what to do, "we" become _responsible_ for what they do: and the "potential regulators" are suddenly interested in who "we" are.

To everyone else, the presumption of a hypothetical censor _creates_ this censor: a centralised component in an otherwise decentralised process.  We need to say as little as possible about the moderation issue and simply tell tooling providers they are conveying / displaying / propagating user generated content.  Each tooling provider will have their own notion of liability and we cannot afford for this to be either our technical or our legal concern.

#### Capitalisation of key terms

To avoid unnecessary edits, and therefore checksum changes, constitution authors MUST follow the following standard English capitalisation rules unless a translation language indicates otherwise:

`Constitution` vs. `constitution`

Something I don't think you mention is the choice of which end of the bytestring you pad or truncate at.  I'd assumed that padding would happen on the left, but in fact you do it on the right. Is the motivation here that it's similar to (or at least compatible with) the way various `zip` functions work in Haskell?  I think that that's perhaps implicit in some of the things you mention later, but it might be worth explaining the justification explicitly.

I'd hope that in many applications all of the bytestrings would be of the same length anyway, so this point would become moot.

One advantage of failing is that you'd find out immediately if something's the wrong length.  When padding/truncation happens automatically a single input of the wrong length in a long chain of calculations will propagate through to the very end and it might be difficult to work out where the problem originated.  That's just a comment however: I'm not going to insist that the choice made here is the wrong one.

Limit orders wouldn't be the ones taking advantage of this, because they're long lived and so can afford the contention; they would be implemented as a UTXO on chain that ensures the user is paid their limit price.

It's market orders that would utilize this; the user would construct a transaction in which the token they are selling doesn't appear in the outputs, but the minimum token they're ok receiving is paid to their address.

An off-chain process then matches them against limit orders, other market orders, or AMM liquidity pools in a validation zone; the minimum output is satisfied by whatever liquidity source, because the user doesn't care where it comes from, and if the tx fails because of contention, they can retry and the users signed tx is still valid.

The limit order contract allows partial matches, enforcing that any surplus is paid back into the contract. Since it's sitting there long term, it can afford the contention: it's other people that are spending it, and it doesn't need to provide a signature.

What we have already implemented in ledger is ordered sets. Commonly an ordered set in math refers to a set with a specified ordering on elements. However, CDDL does not really have a notion of ordering outside of canonical CBOR, which isn't very useful for Cardano anyways. So, I believe it is safe to refer to an `oset` in CDDL as a Set that preserves the order of elements that was supplied in the serialized form of a transaction, which seems like exactly what you are looking for in this CIP

It is true that this design is intended for the case where the initial submitter "needs a certain amount of currency X, and is not ok with getting a lesser amount". The original purpose of this project was paying transaction fees in non-Ada tokens. 

I think it might be possible to support more true DEX-like function, but it would require some extra off-chain communication and complexity. The idea is that users must submit requests alongside the requested amounts, to show that they can cover any funds in the requests that were not exchanged for their desired currency. Then they have to spend some of those funds to cover their own un-exchanged requests. Consider the following change to the DEX aggregator usecase :

1. Parties A1 ... An create transactions T1 ... Tn with requests and offers (unlocked outputs) representing their desired trade, as in the previous example.
              - *here, users actually include the amount they request in the requests, but also provide (in separate data structures D1...Dn) output references which contain enough assets to cover their requests* 
              
2. Parties A1 ... An send T1 ... Tn to B

3. Party B creates two transactions:
    - T(n+1) has fulfilling all the requests in T1 ... Tn, and spends Party B’s liquidity UTXO `u` in order to do so, creating a new entry `u'` with the remainder. It also requires T(n+2)
             - *at this point, there might still be some tokens missing from the zone, if not all requests have been fully covered by zone transaction, so there are some requests in T(n+1) still. The exchange must keep track of which user's requests are being only partially fulfilled* 
    - T(n+2) spends the offers from T1 ... Tn as well as `u'`, creating a new increased liquidity output `u''`
    
4. B sends the unfulfilled requests (in the form of a UTxO set) to the corresponding users , and gets them to sign transactions T' which (i) spend the missing requests that remain after the aggregation, and (ii) spend the outputs in D1...Dn , which contain enough to cover the missing requested amounts

5. All parties check and sign the transaction from B that "refund" the unexchanged funds, send them back to B

6. Party B submits a validation zone consisting of T1 ... T(n+2) ; T'

This is not fully developed usecase yet, but the point is that it uses this infrastructure to to do something that works like partially fulfilling requests.

IIUC these steps introduce a user coordination problem that I think makes this impractical at scale, and will actually create perverse incentives for the aggregator. 

Consider if Alice, Bob, and Charlie all submit off-chain orders as you describe and an aggregator batches them together using Validation Zones. In this batch, all user orders are only partially fulfilled. The aggregator must send the required refund transactions to each user, and wait for them to sign and return the transactions before it can submit the batch.

What if Alice and Bob quickly sign their required refund transactions, but Charlie is unavailable? This would likely mean UTxOs being spent by the batch will be taken by other aggregators/users and this batch transaction is now invalid. Alice and Bob are therefore hurt by Charlie's slow response. This problem will likely happen frequently, especially if this is a global marketplace where all parties are strangers and live in separate time zones. In practice, this means Alice, Bob, and Charlie will need to always be online and quickly sign all refund transactions to maximize the chance of at least one going through. Most of these transactions will likely fail due to the coordination problem. This would be a terrible user experience, and is probably bad enough to deter most people from using this system in the first place.

This is also bad from the aggregator perspective since the aggregator likely only gets paid if the batched transactions are successfully submitted. The more partial users the aggregator tries to batch together, the more the coordination problem will be an issue. To minimize this risk, aggregators will either batch the minimum number of partial users required, or simply avoid any partial filling of orders to avoid the coordination problem entirely.

I think I actually came up with an approach to partial matching that doesn't require any changes to the Validation Zone design and also doesn't require "breaking off" pieces of on-chain liquidity sources. AFAICT all of the approaches described so far have been from the perspective of matching each off-chain intent against an on-chain liquidity source UTxO. However, it may be more practical to match off-chain intents against each other and *only match the value difference against an on-chain liquidity source*. This approach has the benefit of being able to "on-load" partial fulfillment to the on-chain liquidity sources without having to break up the on-chain liquidity UTxOs.

For a simple example, imagine if Alice has 10 ADA and wants to convert it to 9 DJED. She already has the 10 ADA sitting in a UTxO so she just needs to create the intent transaction, sign it, and send it to an aggregator. This UTxO with 10 ADA will be the fulfilling output for her intent transaction.

Meanwhile, Bob has 8 DJED and wants to convert it to 9 ADA. Like Alice, he already has the 8 DJED in a UTxO so he can just create the intent transaction, sign it, and send it to an aggregator. This UTxO with 8 DJED will be the fulfilling output for his intent transaction.

The aggregator sees the two intent transactions, but can't match them because the values don't match exactly: there is a net value difference of +1 ADA (10 ADA input - 9 ADA output) and -1 DJED (8 DJED input - 9 DJED output). This is the double coincidence of wants problem, but it is easily solvable by using an on-chain liquidity source to convert the extra 1 ADA to 1 DJED. On-chain liquidity sources can be partially fulfilled so it would be easy to find a liquidity source to use.

So the aggregator matches the two intents against each other and matches the value difference against the on-chain liquidity source to produce a valid transaction. The required fulfilling outputs for the intent transactions *already exist* so there is no need for the aggregator to try breaking off pieces of the on-chain liquidity UTxO.

I think this approach works especially well for on-chain liquidity sources that can be composed. For example, if Alice wanted to convert ADA -> WMT and Bob wanted to convert AGIX -> ADA, these two off-chain intents can't be directly matched against each other. However, if there is a liquidity source for AGIX -> USDC and another for USDC -> WMT, the off-chain intents can be indirectly matched together as long as the on-chain liquidity sources can be composed to effectively create a AGIX -> WMT conversion. So this transaction would have 2 off-chain intents + 2 on-chain liquidity sources. It is even possible to batch different pairings of intents+sources as long as the liquidity sources can be composed in the same transaction.

From an incentives perspective, aggregators will actually want to do this, even without charging a fee, because the possible compositions enable finding huge arbitrage opportunities. It is possible for no collateral to ever be at risk with this approach (it depends on the liquidity source logic). I explained these incentives in-depth in my cardano-swaps DEX [readme](https://github.com/fallen-icarus/cardano-swaps?tab=readme-ov-file#naturally-incentivized-liquidity) which uses the same arbitrage possibilities to incentivize aggregators.

This approach also enables users to submit limit orders off-chain, and allows them to update their asking prices off-chain as well (the day-trading use case). The user would need to trust the aggregator to use the newest intent transaction, but all of the cancellation methods mentioned in the CIP would still work with this method so users can revoke permission at any time.

This should work even if you can't match the intents against each other. If there were 10 intents for ADA -> DJED, they can be matched against a single liquidity source UTxO as long as each intent creator already has the required fulfilling output ready. It isn't necessary to have one liquidity source UTxO per intent; all that matters is all fulfilling outputs are present and the overall value is balanced.
