@polinavino I appreciate you continuing to answer my questions regarding this CIP! It seems I've been misunderstanding how intents are ultimately modeled in Validation Zones. The more I learn about Validation Zones, the more its design seems to diverge from the way I've always thought Cardano intents would work.

> ### Open (atomic) swaps
>
> A wants to swap 10 Ada for 5 tokens `myT`.
>
> 1. Party `A` creates a transaction `tx1` with
>    - an unlocked request `0` with 5 `myT` tokens,
>    - some inputs totalling 10 Ada
>    - an output `0` which contains 5 `myT` tokens, and
>    - an unlocked output `1` containing 10 Ada
> 
> -- *reordered to group inputs with outputs*

AFIAU Validation Zones model intents as *completed transactions*, albeit with some holes to fill (the CIP calls these "underspecified transactions"). The above transaction (`tx1`) is fully balanced and specifies *exactly* what each input/output should look like:
- only one extra input is allowed and it must contain 5 `myT`
- only one extra output is allowed and it must contain 10 Ada

But this is not what an intent *actually* is. An intent is just a *piece* of a transaction. This is perfectly exemplified by the above descriptor: `A wants to swap 10 Ada for 5 tokens myT`. This doesn't say anything about the other pieces of the transaction. In the atomic swap above, the intent is more accurately modeled by just:
> - some inputs totalling 10 Ada
> - an output `0` which contains  5 `myT` tokens

The other unlocked input (aka request) and unlocked output in `tx1` do nothing but restrict how this intent can be used:
- You cannot combine intents into a single transaction since they are already complete transactions. Instead, Validation Zones enables batching transactions but this adds cost to the aggregator since each transaction has a minimum 0.15 ADA fee. The fact that all Validation Zone intents are separate transactions means this cost can quickly add up.
- You cannot perform other actions in the intent transaction, even if the intent owner is actually okay with it. If Alice just wants the above atomic swap, she doesn't care if the aggregator also satisfies someone else's intent in the same transaction. The aggregator could also do a swap of their own and Alice still wouldn't care. Forcing each intent to be an isolated transaction seems like a waste of space and money.
- The intent owner has to *guess* what the missing inputs and outputs would look like and place these holes in the transaction. If they guess wrong, this places enormous friction (aka, increased cost) on how an aggregator can actually fulfill this intent. Specifically, the aggregator must contort (ie, break up or merge) other UTxOs to fit the holes set in each intent. The batched transactions in Validation Zones is also meant to address this, but this means the previous bullets are exacerbated since each Validation Zone intent actually requires *multiple* transactions to fulfill it.

I think the eUTxO model actually enables modeling intents more closely to what they are: *pieces of transactions*. Alice can create a piece of a transaction, sign it, and send it to the aggregator. Bob can do the same. The aggregator can take these two transaction pieces and fit them together monoidally (ie, like a puzzle) to create a full transaction. I am making an important assumption here: **a collection of *signed* transaction pieces is just as valid as a single transaction signed by everyone**. I don't see how aggregating the pieces would invalidate the signatures. The fact that each UTxO is atomic seems to guarantee each piece can be considered an *independent event*. This is effectively a multisig where each party only needs to sign the parts of the transaction that are actually relevant to them. It is a *decentralized multisig*.

An empty transaction piece is effectively just a transaction with all fields empty. Users can add pieces they care about and leave the rest blank. So for the above atomic swap, Alice can create a transaction piece with one input from her address for 10 ADA and one output to her address for 5 `myT`; everything else is left empty. Bob can create his intent with one input, 2 outputs, and a validity interval; everything else is left blank. As long as there are no conflicts between the pieces, these two pieces can be fit together to create a transaction with 2 inputs, 3 outputs, and the validity interval from Bob's intent. The aggregator can even add their own piece to the mix to finish balancing it. If Alice and Bob each signed their respective pieces, why does it matter what else happens in the transaction? Alice's input is still only spendable if she gets her output in the same transaction. 

When the completed transaction is submitted, the ledger would verify the transaction is a valid combination of all of the pieces and all pieces are properly witnessed. The pieces and their signatures would need to be somewhere in the transaction. Since the overall transaction can be derived from the pieces, the CDDL can be redesigned around this idea.

For smart contracts, users can specify mints, observers, staking scripts, etc, in there respective pieces. However, unlike how pubkey signatures only need to sign their respective pieces, the smart contracts would be executed against the aggregated (aka completed) transaction. This means smart contracts can even be used to *disallow* certain combinations of intent pieces.

Cancellation would work the same way as in Validation Zones. Just include a reference input or normal input in your transaction piece. To cancel it, just spend the input. These transaction pieces can even contain input "holes" (ie, unspecified output references for certain inputs). I personally don't see a need for output holes; they seem to have been introduced into Validation Zones just to compensate for its restrictiveness.
 
This approach even seems much cleaner to use for Babel Fees. For example, imagine if Alice wants to buy a sword NFT worth 25 GEMS and the transaction fee is worth about 1.4 GEMS (total of 26.4 GEMS). If Alice has a UTxO with 30 GEMS, she can create an intent piece that only specifies an input from her address for 30 GEMS and an output to her address for 3.6 GEMS + the sword NFT; all other parts are left empty. She would sign this piece and send it to the game devs who can now batch Alice's intent piece with other users who also want to purchase game items. Since these intent pieces can easily be combined, it is possible for the game devs to sell a variety of game NFTs to multiple, unrelated users in a single transaction. Doing the same thing with Validation Zones seems overly complicated and expensive (many transactions are required).

I'm not sure of everything that would need to change to support transaction pieces, but on the surface it seems way more expressive and more cost effective than Validation Zones. It doesn't seem like anyone has considered breaking up transactions and signing the pieces like this. I recognize this is probably a major change, but the expressiveness may make it entirely worth it. Is there some reason why it wouldn't work?

The way I am thinking about it, the role token requirement is guaranteed to be true; there is no way to NOT spend the role token. No "resolving" is required.

A zone is just a list of transaction: `[tx1, tx2, tx3]`. But we can force a dimension of time on the list:
```
---- Time ---->
[tx1, tx2, tx3]
```

If we do this, then the above is just a mini-blockchain, and we can treat it as such. The zone can build up its own mini UTxO set, and transactions in the zone have access to the current state of `real UTxO set + zone UTxO set` at the time they are being processed. The zone can keep track of both the UTxOs spent from the real UTxO set and the UTxOs created/spent from the zone UTxO set. When all transactions in the zone have been fully validated, the net affect of the real UTxO set + the zone UTxO set is what actually gets applied to the blockchain.

In the above zone, `tx1` gets processed first. Imagine if `tx1` spends a real output `r1` and produces an output `z1`. The zone would log that `r1` has been spent from the real UTxO set and `z1` has been added to the zone UTxO set. `tx2` comes after `tx1` and can spend any remaining UTxO in the real UTxO set and the zone UTxO set. So `tx2` cannot spend `r1` because it was already spent by `tx1`, but it can spend both `r2` (another input from the real set) and `z1` to produce `z2`. `tx2` would call `z1` explicitly by output reference: `(hash(tx1), z1_index)`. `z1_index` is its index in `tx1`'s output list.

Now the new state is the real UTxO set minus `r1` and `r2`, plus the zone UTxO set of `z2`. `tx3` comes after `tx2` so it must use this new state. If it wants to spend `z2`, it must call it explicitly by output reference: `(hash(tx2), z2_index)`. `z2_index` is its index in `tx2`'s output list. Let's say `tx3` spends `z2` and produces `z3`. `tx3` cannot spend `z1` because it was already spent by `tx2`.

The net effect of this zone is `r1` and `r2` are both spent to produce `z3`. This is the change that would actually be recorded on the blockchain. 

With this method, if the role token was in `r1`, `tx1` moved it to `z1`. If `tx2` wants to execute the smart contract that requires the role token, it must now spend `z1` because that is where the token is at the time `tx2` is being processed. If `tx3` wants to use the role token as well, it must spend `z2` since that is where `tx2` moved the token to. Because time is enforced on the zone, the zone can know where the role token is at all times. When `z3` is actually recorded on-chain, it is the result of `r1` -> `z1` -> `z2` -> `z3`. The eUTxO model guarantees the result is the same as doing the updates separately (ie, in separate zones).

> [!Important]
> With this approach, building a transaction chain **requires** coordination between the transactions in the chain. However, I am making the assertion that: *coordination is always possible whenever transaction chaining is useful*.  If we accept this assertion, there is no need for any "resolving", and flash loans are impossible.

Strangers can't build up chains this way since they don't know each others' transactions (and therefore each others' output references), but why would strangers be chaining their transactions anyway? This is mainly useful for account style DApps that are controlled by batchers.

A batcher can personally build up the chain when trying to fulfill the user orders. They can create `tx1` first and use its hash in `tx2`, and then use `tx2`'s hash in `tx3`. Furthermore, since the batcher knows the order of the outputs in each transaction, they know what the resulting output references will be in advance. The batcher can even turn the user orders into chains (if the user transactions allow for it). If batchers need to build up a chain together, they can coordinate this off-chain.

Because the outputs are being called explicitly by output reference, it is trivial to check if the role token is actually being spent. The smart contracts don't even need to know they are being executed in a zone.

The collateral mechanism (for the purpose of preventing a DDoS) must guarantee that : 
- a node must be compensated for running all scripts that are run by that node as part of (phase-2) validation of an (already phase-1 valid) transaction 
- it is not possible to change the outcome of script validation for scripts in a transaction without changing and re-signing it

There is no guarantee that a single transaction is valid in a zone (since it may be unbalanced). Consider a valid zone [Tx1 ; Tx2]  : 

Tx1 is 
- unbalanced,
- executes S1, S1 succeeds
- provides collateral for only S1

Tx2 is 
- unbalanced 
- executes S2, S2 fails
- provides collateral for only S2

Zone [Tx1 ; Tx2] cannot be added as is, since Tx1 is unbalanced, and the collateral of Tx2 does not balance the zone! 

What we do instead is apply *only* the failing transaction, Tx2, when adding this zone, and only by collecting its collateral. BUT the node executed a (possibly very big and complicated S1) - who pays for this? It has to be Tx2's collateral, since no other transactions are processed in the zone. So, Tx2 has to pay for all transactions that have been validated before it. Note here that if someone inserts a transaction *before* Tx2 into this zone, then a node will see that Tx2 does not have enough collateral, and immediately discard this as an invalid zone. 

If we say there is a special Tx3 that provides *collateral only*, this prevents other users from adding more transactions to the zone after the only-collateral transaction is inserted, AND this forces nodes to not validate any transactions at all in the case a zone is not complete (i.e. the collateral transaction is not yet added) - since no collateral is available for its validation.

Note that the expected usecases here are atomic swaps, or dex aggregators, or dApp sponsorship. In all of these cases, we would expect that the user adding subsequent transactions has the capacity to provide the required collateral, and can locally check that they will not lose it no matter how zone construction proceeds thereafter.

> The problem with having a single collateral for a zone is, again, the fact that if someone adds a transaction with failing scripts to a zone, the collateral would be taken **(again, with no detriment to the adder of the bad transaction)**, and whoever added that collateral will have no power to stop this.

This is not true. **The only person who needs to be punished is the aggregator that batched and submitted the zone.** It is trivial for the aggregator to run the zone locally to verify the zone will succeed. There is no reason for an aggregator to ever add a transaction to the batch that will fail. IMO "the adder of the bad transaction" is **always** the aggregator. How *could* it be anyone else? The aggregator is the only entity that should put up collateral.

> Note that the expected usecases here are atomic swaps, or dex aggregators, or dApp sponsorship.

These are not the only use cases. With eUTxO style DApps, Alice may want to execute one as part of her intent. **Alice is not the aggregator** in this scenario. This is not possible with the current design because Alice does not know where in the order of the zone her intent will appear. It is literally impossible for her to know how much collateral to provide for the preceding transactions.

With the approach I mentioned, only one transaction in the zone needs to have collateral. The best transaction for this is the one the aggregator creates to finish balancing the zone. It will include enough collateral to cover **all scripts in the zone**. All transactions that come before this last transaction do not need to specify collateral. In every use case, the aggregator can add a final transaction to the zone.

> The collateral mechanism (for the purpose of preventing a DDoS) must guarantee that :
>
>  - a node must be compensated for running all scripts that are run by that node as part of (phase-2) validation of an (already phase-1 valid) transaction
> - it is not possible to change the outcome of script validation for scripts in a transaction without changing and re-signing it

Both of these guarantees are still satisfied. To use your example:
Tx1 is
- unbalanced
- executes S1, S1 succeeds
- **no collateral is specified**

Tx2 is
- unbalanced
- executes S2, S2 fails
- **provides enough collateral for S1 and S2**

In the above scenario, all of the collateral from Tx2 is taken. In an alternate scenario where S1 fails, and therefore S2 is never run, **all of the collateral from Tx2 is still taken**. It would not matter that the collateral is over-paid in the scenario that S1 fails. Again, the aggregator could have easily caught this failure by running the zone locally. Since it is their negligence, **they are the only one who should get punished**.

> BUT the node executed a (possibly very big and complicated S1) - who pays for this? It has to be Tx2's collateral, since **no other transactions are processed in the zone**. So, Tx2 has to pay for all transactions that have been validated before it.
-- emphasis mine

AFAIU the emphasized part is just an arbitrary design choice. In the case of a failed script, I see no reason why **all** transactions in the zone can't be processed in order to claim all specified collateral. No scripts need to be run in order to claim collateral. If Tx1 did specify collateral, the total collateral taken would be Tx1 collateral + Tx2 collateral, no matter which script in the zone fails.

By allowing intents to specify no collateral, **intent creators won't risk their own collateral because they are incentivized not to**. This then forces all aggregators to effectively pledge that the zone is valid since they are required to add a final transaction with the collateral even if the zone is already balanced. This is a better alignment of incentives since the aggregator is the one that actually batches and submits the zone. Whose fault is it that a node is trying to process a zone that has a failed script? This is always the aggregator's fault; they could have just omitted the intent transaction with the failing script.

In VZ design, is possible to allow for the special cases where some nodes would be willing to cover collateral of other users by signing users transactions that include the use of their collateral UTxOs, taking on the risk. This should be the exception and not the rule, however.

> I am not sure if this is better or worse than just having lists of lists, but so far we didnt foresee a problem with the change

You didn't see this because that is the work that would be coming from the consensus side. Support from ledger will be needed, but that is why you did not run into this problem yet.

> This lets scripts see into other transaction bodies, but does not force this.

I am not really sure that this is a good idea. This approach of sometimes allowing the script to see only some of the transactions in the zone feels a bit arbitrary. Let's say you have a script that requires you to specify other transactions in the zone, but there is only one occasion when you can supply all of them, because there will be other transactions that depends on the transaction you are building in the zone. For example, only the final transaction in the zone has this ability to supply all of the transactions in the zone, therefore such script could only be used in the final transaction. From the perspective of balancing transactions there are no real dependencies between transactions in the zone, that process is 100% commutative. Therefore I am not convinced that `requiredTxs` is a good idea at all. 

> Yes, this is just for ease of handling transaction construction from a user's perspective

Yep, makes sense.


> Transactions do not depend on each other inside a zone in any way unless one specifies another's ID in the requiredTxs field

There is implicit DAG dependency through the collateral requirement.

I guess my overall comparison would be something like : 

VZ and Swaps do : 
- reduce duplication of witnesses 
- support exchanges with counterparty irrelevance 
- allow scripts to see other Txs 
- allow others to pay your fees
- require some sophisticated-ish off-chain infrastructure

VZ negatives : 
- need to construct zones
- mempool needs to deal with zones
- more fiddly

VZ positives : 
- does not impose transaction dependencies unless specified by the user
- any DAG dependency graph is allowed rather than *-dependency , which is more versatile 
- collateral mechanism still works for DDoS
- collateral required for only your own scripts (unless dependencies specified) 
- individual collateral slightly cheaper because only the scripts in one transaction with failing scripts ever need to be run/covered by collateral
- Plutus scripts will be slightly cheaper to run, because other transactions' data is only shown to them when required by user

> There is implicit DAG dependency through the collateral requirement.

No, this is no longer true. Only cover your own collateral. This was a legacy requirement from previous design, as I realized. Because that design allowed for transactions to spend each-others outputs within a single zone.

> For example, only the final transaction in the zone has this ability to supply all of the transactions in the zone, therefore such script could only be used in the final transaction. 

Yea, this is the DAG dependency. If you want to show a script a transaction, that transaction has to have been constructed already. This is similar to the top-level transaction in your case showing swaps to the scripts in it, but not the other way around. However, scripts aren't forced to see those other transactions.

Providing collateral fro all preceding transactions made sense to me. This change that everyone specifies their own collateral raises this questions:

say we have theses txs in the zone: `[tx1, tx2, tx3, tx4]`

While the nodes validates all these transactions in this sequence and only `tx3` fails phase2 validation then is the collateral collected for all of the transactions in the zone or just the ones that have already been validated or just the one that failed?

None of the decisions who pays the collateral is fair as far as I can understand it.

requiredTx does not guarantee fairness either.

Say this is the zone: 
```
[ tx1a <- tx2a <- tx3a
, tx1b
, tx1c <- tx2c
]
```
`a`, `b` and `c` groups provide their own collateral for the group. What happens to the whole zone when only `tx1b` fails phase2 validation?

Collateral for group `a` is not gonna be collected, but the node did the work validating that dependency group.

As a node that runs the babel-fee service, you get a transaction with a failing script, you put that on-chain with its `requiredTxs` purely for collateral collection, as a zone. If it was meant to complete an existing zone, that zone is still incomplete, and awaiting other transactions to complete it. However, you've already validated its scripts, but are waiting on new (valid) transactions to complete the zone, you don't need to re-validate them. 

As a node that is simply processing blocks, you don't even validate scripts in any transactions in a phase-2 invalid zone *except* for the single phase-2 invalid tx, whose scripts you check to make sure they do indeed fail.

First, you do phase-1 checks, which includes checking that exactly 0 or 1 transactions in a zone are labeleld as `isValid = False`. Then 

- if no transactions are `isValid` False, all scripts should succeed (unless its a bad block and that's bad)
- if 1 tx has `isValid` False, you only run the scripts in that transaction, not in any of its dependents. You just pass the dependent transactions as `TxInfo` to those scripts (to check that they fail)

The `tx-submission` mini-protocol has a few other protocol invariants which are enforced but not visible at the type / protocol level.  I think we want to mention them here in a separate section.

## Outbound Side
* blocking request must be done IFF the buffer of unacknowledged `id`-s is empty (this also means that one cannot do a non-blocking request if the unacknowledged `id`-s buffer is empty)
* one cannot request `0` `id`s either through a blocking or a non-blocking request 

## Inbound Side
* it is a protocol error to send `message` which `id` wasn't requested

The MSM implementation is quite complicated in blst, but if I understood the code correctly, [that](https://github.com/supranational/blst/blob/415d4f0e2347a794091836a3065206edfd9c72f3/src/multi_scalar.c#L60) comment says about different thing. It compares two-step msm procedure and Pippenger algorithm, which seems to be somewhat different algorithms.

Mentioned two-step MSM with pre-computation is implemented by [`ptype##s_precompute_wbits`](https://github.com/supranational/blst/blob/415d4f0e2347a794091836a3065206edfd9c72f3/src/multi_scalar.c#L122) and [`ptype##s_mult_wbits`](https://github.com/supranational/blst/blob/415d4f0e2347a794091836a3065206edfd9c72f3/src/multi_scalar.c#L179).
It allows to pre-compute a table for a fixed set of points and then reuse it for MSM with different sets of scalars, in which case it is faster than Pippenger. On the other hand, the [Pippenger procedure](https://github.com/supranational/blst/blob/415d4f0e2347a794091836a3065206edfd9c72f3/src/multi_scalar.c#L352) is a different algo which doesn't allow passing the pre-computed table. 
Even more confusing is that the exposed library call for [Pippenger](https://github.com/supranational/blst/blob/415d4f0e2347a794091836a3065206edfd9c72f3/src/multi_scalar.c#L397) internally makes a [selection](https://github.com/supranational/blst/blob/415d4f0e2347a794091836a3065206edfd9c72f3/src/multi_scalar.c#L408) between the two-step MSM (without table re-usability) and pure Pippenger (I guess this is what they referred to by [last phrase in the comment](https://github.com/supranational/blst/blob/415d4f0e2347a794091836a3065206edfd9c72f3/src/multi_scalar.c#L70)).

The difference between two-step MSM with precompute and Pippenger can be clearly observed in [C++ bindings](https://github.com/supranational/blst/blob/master/bindings/blst.hpp#L418). It provides a convenient interface to use both methods. On the other hand Rust bindings defaults to use only [Pippenger](https://github.com/supranational/blst/blob/415d4f0e2347a794091836a3065206edfd9c72f3/src/multi_scalar.c#L397) procedure without providing high-level API for two-step MSM with pre computation (although it is still accessible through exposed C functions).

On top of all of that Rust bindings implement its own optimizations with parallelization. In case of more than 2 CPUs and <32 points it defaults to naive parallelized [implementation](https://github.com/supranational/blst/blob/master/bindings/rust/src/pippenger.rs#L165). This I believe the cause of time peculiarity at the bound of 32 point. And given how drastically time is improved after 32, I'm not sure this optimization is worthwhile (but it probably depends on how many CPUs are present).

All in all, for Haskell implementation I would suggest to stick to the [implementation](https://github.com/supranational/blst/blob/master/bindings/rust/src/pippenger.rs#L133) provided by Rust bindings and just reimplement it in Haskell but with careful consideration whether we need this <32 points naive optimization.

I'd like to suggest an alternative approach that leverages the [distributed DApp design](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/pull/466). The idea is to give everyone their own DApp address - all addresses use the same plutus script for the payment credential and use a personal staking credential. Then, assets within a DApp address can only be sent to other addresses for that DApp.

Consider an "art vault" DApp that is meant to hold a user's art NFT collection. If Alice wants to send her SpaceBudz NFT (which is located inside her art vault) to Bob, she must send the NFT to Bob's art vault (the vault DApp address using Bob's staking credential). Trying to send the NFT to a non-vault address should fail.

This approach effectively creates a sub-ledger that can manage its own state in a distributed manor, and it enables adding configurable "controls" on how assets are traded between the DApp's addresses. For example, with the art vault DApp, every transfer can enforce a royalty payment; this would enable the cardano settlement layer to naturally enforce royalties. To do this, every transaction that spends an NFT from within the art vault "network" must reference the required input that contains the royalty information for that NFT (using something like [CIP-68](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/tree/master/CIP-0068)). The vault DApp would enforce the required royalties seen in the referenced input. I actually created a proof-of-concept of this a while ago, but had to put it aside due to time constraints (the documentation isn't complete).

Using the distributed approach, you can also freeze assets/addresses. The distributed DApp could require all transactions to reference a particular input (or set of inputs) and if it is missing or configured a certain way, the transaction is guaranteed to fail. These required reference inputs can be governed by some entity. So a stablecoin issuer can have a centrally controlled reference input that has a list of blacklisted addresses; any transaction that tries to spend from/to these addresses can be made to fail.

The benefits of the distributed approach are:
1. More scalable since you don't need to carry around global state with every transaction. All state is local.
2. The state is naturally enforced by the Cardano Blockchain - in other words, a transfer from Alice to Bob is already enforced/secured by Cardano. Instead, the distributed DApp just needs to ensure the assets can't inappropriately leave the DApp address network.
3. Other DApps can more easily "see" the current state for a user since the state is local. The local state makes it significantly easier for the distributed DApp to compose with other DApps. Compare this to smart contracts needing to look at the global state for everyone, including users not relevant to the transaction.

This CIP does not necessarily suffer from 1 and 3, but it does suffer from 2 since dedicated transfer logic is required to update the ledger modeled by the datums.

The most important use-case for this builtin data-structure is to facilitate fast operations over the `Value` type defined as `Map.Map CurrencySymbol (Map.Map TokenName Integer)`. These operations are by far one of the biggest performance bottlenecks for onchain code. 

It is extremely expensive to apply validation logic to `Value`s in onchain code because of the high cost of map operations. `union` is by far the most expensive value operation, but it also used nearly universally by dApps and is a huge performance bottleneck. This builtin data-structure needs to have a semigroup collision handling for `Values` either `unionBSMap` with some bool flag indicating a value or just a separate `unionBSMapValue` builtin for use with `Value` types.

The common pattern shared across most protocols is as follows:

1. Given an input, construct the value expected to be possessed by the output which seeks to satisfy the spending conditions of said input.
2. Check that the expected output value matches the actual output value 

The construction of the expected output value is in the majority of cases a union of the input value and a value delta (the quantities of 
assets to be added to / removed from the input, ie. the difference in value between the input UTxO and the output UTxO).

```haskell
processRequest :: ProtocolStateDatum -> TxInInfo -> TxOut -> Bool 
processRequest stateDatum txIn txOut = 
  let resolvedInput = (txInInfoResolved txIn)
      inputValue = txOutValue resolvedInput
      outputValue = txOutValue txOut
      -- Given a tx input and the relevant state datum compute the value delta between the input value 
      -- and the expected value delta between the input value and the expected. (ie the quantities of 
      -- assets to be added to / removed from the input.  
      inputValueDelta = computeValueDelta txIn stateDatum 
      expectedOutputValue = inputValue <> inputValueDelta
   in expectedOutputValue == outputValue
```

The idea was that the peras certificate would be significantly smaller than the block size so that block producers would fill in the remaining bytes and just propagate the block normally, so there should not be an impact on block diffusion, only on tx inclusion in case this happens while the mempools are congested. 

Note that inclusion of certificates in blocks will be an extremely rare event. In the worst case, assuming nodes immediately enter cooldown when they are back from it, this means 1 Peras certificate roughly every 3000 blocks. In normal operations, this could be much rarer as we expect quorum will be reached on every round.

It does not seem to us the resources requirements for Peras would incur significant additional costs to SPOs, but of course this should be assessed more carefully. We could imagine some specific incentive scheme to reward participation to Peras but the situation here is different than with Mithril: Peras changes the consensus and therefore has to be part of the core node operations.

That said, it's possible to start rolling out Peras as a sidecar and make blocks certificates informational, e.g something anyone connected to the network would observe and decide whether or not it's relevant. If you observe that 75% of nodes running Peras endorsed a specific block, even though this is not baked in the consensus you can already assume this block has a much stronger  likelihood of not being rolledback.

ALBA certificates sample the votes' set so we could not use that to assess whether or not a particular SPO participated in Peras.

Hi @Ryun1,

This CIP outlines a generic approach to dynamic, decentralized NFT minting and burning within the constraints of the EUTxO model. The idea is to store a compact representation of an off-chain dataset as the state on-chain.

Therefore, different implementations, such as:

[Sparse Merkle Tree (SMT)](https://github.com/aiken-lang/sparse-merkle-tree)
[Merkle Patricia Forestry (MPF)](https://github.com/aiken-lang/merkle-patricia-forestry)
[BLS-based Plutus Accumulator](https://github.com/perturbing/plutus-accumulator)
can all follow the same core principles.

For my specific implementation, I’m using a complete binary tree, which I’ve named `IntegriTree`. You can explore the [technical details](https://github.com/ilap/adatag/blob/main/doc/TECHSPEC.md) on its [GitHub repo](https://github.com/ilap/adatag), and there’s a working demo available on the Preview Network at [adatag.io](https://adatag.io/). Please note that the code has not been audited.

To summarize:

The proposal offers a general solution/recommendation for dynamic NFT minting.
Different use cases can adopt various implementations, but, to my knowledge, all of them would need to follow the principles outlined in this CIP.

The state is stored on-chain, and state transitions occur by submitting a minting/burning transaction that includes 
- the old state as an **input**'s  inline datum,
- the new state as an **output**'s inline datum, 
- and a proof as a max 5KB long **redeemer**, that verifies the validity of the addition or removal of an element from the set. 

Conceptually, it works like:
`newState == Prove(proof, oldState, element, add or remove)`. 

Meaning, burning/minting occurs if this—and other validation checks—are valid.

Here is an image of the complete transaction (state transition from the initial state) example from my MVP/PoC implementation.

![Complete Transaction.](https://github.com/ilap/adatag/blob/main/contracts/aiken/images/AdatagTransaction.drawio.png?raw=true)

Sorry, my suggestion had a flaw, the ordering should be like this:

```haskell
indexArray :: (() -> a) -> Array a -> Integer -> a
```

This is so that we can

1. give a name to `indexArray (\_ -> error)` (e.g. `unsafeIndexArray`) and recover the failing version of `indexArray` that way without pretty much any performance overhead (that application will be computed once per execution)
2. give a name to `unsafeIndexArray arr` for a specific `arr`, so that this application also needs to be computed only once

1.  CIP-105 defines bech32 identifiers with the key (CC hot, CC cold, DREP) and credential (script hash, public key hash) defined by the bech32 prefix only.  In CIP-105 the binary payload for the bech32 encoding is always just the key material itself.

The abstract sets an ambitious goal by suggesting that this CIP provides a "truly decentralized alternative to KYC." However, the solution proposed—an Affirmation Graph—is probabilistic and does not provide guarantees about a wallet's authenticity or trustworthiness. While the system introduces a novel approach to building decentralized trust relationships, it falls short of delivering the full equivalence of KYC.

Two specific concerns arise from this:

**Overstating the Solution's Capabilities**: The current wording creates the impression that the Affirmation Graph is a comprehensive replacement for KYC. This could lead to a false sense of security for users who might overestimate its reliability.

**Unclear Goal Alignment**: If the system inherently cannot guarantee trust, what is the purpose of framing it as an alternative to KYC? A more accurate framing might describe it as a tool for probabilistic trust evaluation rather than a replacement for centralized identity verification.

A possible rephrasing of the opening could be:

"This CIP defines a decentralized mechanism to establish probabilistic trust relationships between wallets, providing a step toward alternatives to centralized KYC mechanisms."

This revision would better align with the proposal's actual capabilities while setting realistic expectations for its use. Additionally, it might be helpful to include a disclaimer in the abstract to caution readers about the limitations of probabilistic trust mechanisms, ensuring transparency and reducing the risk of misuse.

The statement about using an algorithm to assign trust rankings introduces a potential vulnerability. If the specific algorithm used to assign trust values to wallets becomes widely known, it could be exploited or “gamed” by malicious actors. This could lead to manipulated trust rankings, undermining the reliability of the system.

This issue becomes particularly problematic if users develop a false sense of security, assuming that the trust rankings are inherently reliable or immune to manipulation.

The claim that this CIP could "drastically reduce the risk of fraud and accidental loss of funds" feels overstated. While it makes trust evaluations more systematic and repeatable, it does not eliminate risks like system manipulation or false trust. A more balanced phrasing might highlight that it complements manual diligence rather than fully replacing it.

Something like

*"This CIP proposes a decentralized mechanism for assessing wallet trustworthiness in a systematic and repeatable way, aiming to reduce the effort and inconsistencies of manual evaluations. While it does not eliminate risk entirely, it provides a new tool to complement existing approaches to fraud prevention."*
While I agree with the sentiment of the statement, this CIP does not actually propose a solution for providing such an ID, making the inclusion of this line somewhat misleading.

The claim of a "simple, truly decentralized mechanism for identity verification and trust" feels overstated. Based on the issues raised in my earlier comments, this CIP provides a mechanism for probabilistic trust relationships, which is not equivalent to robust identity verification. A more accurate phrasing might clarify that it offers a decentralized tool for assessing trust rather than verifying identity outright.

While I understand the desire for an alternative to stake-weighted voting, I believe this solution is not suited as a foundation for governance voting. Given the outlined security concerns and the probabilistic nature of this system, it can only serve as a complementary tool, not a reliable basis for ensuring fair and secure voting.

Perhaps I should explicitly state that we're basically treating stake keys as DiDs here, and a stake key with a high trust rating is a form of ID in itself. I do understand the potential for confusion here though so I will clarify.

It does also support robust identity verification in the form of affirmations by KYC providers. In fact it makes these KYC verifications portable so that you only need to do KYC once and it's portable to any dApp on Cardano.
That said, I take your point about overpromising, and will scale back some of the grand claims ;)

The devil is really in the detail of how you interpret the graph - in the most simple case where you're basically just adding 1 to the trust score for every affirmation that a wallet has - there's definite potential for abuse with that. However, in a lot of cases, that might be "good enough". 
The real power comes when you start weighting affirmations based on various criteria. As mentioned, you could only give any weight at all to affirmations from centralized KYC services - this enables portable KYC, so you only have to do KYC once on Cardano and then all dApps can see that you've done it. I will probably write a further specification around these centralized KYC->Affirmation services, as they will attach metadata to the affirmation enabling the KYC to be traced if necessary. 

The exciting bit for me is when you start building complex algorithms for interpreting the graph - the Affirmation Graph indexer that I'm building gives quite a lot of information that can be used to inform these algorithms. For example, the date when every affirmation occurred, the date of a each wallet's first ever transaction (of any kind), smart contracts that wallet has interacted with (and frequency), native tokens held by that wallet etc. So this would enable you to implement certain safeguards - say, de-weighting affirmations from any newly created wallet. You can also use graph theory to detect new clusters, or isolated clusters that are not strongly interwoven with the rest of the graph. You could also detect unusual behaviour that might result from a compromised wallet - for example if a wallet suddenly starts issuing lots of affirmations outside their own local cluster, and to relatively new or untrusted wallets.

Members of the various factional communities on Cardano (mostly centred around NFT projects) will be able to bias their judgements in favour of members of their own community - giving their affirmations a higher weight. OR you could choose to ignore the opinion of anyone who holds a particular meme coin that you may dislike. 

The power is in allowing people to design their own graph interpretation algorithm - I may even create a visual algorithm-builder, such that even non-technical users will be able to design and customize their own algorithm, and encode their own personal biases within it. 

I have also thought about using machine learning to further augment the safeguards - once the graph is established and we have some examples of good and bad actors, it might make sense to train an AI to detect bad actors. It might even be capable of predicting rug pulls before they happen. However, I'm personally philosophically a bit wary of bringing AI into what is basically a social experiment on trust - it could get dystopian pretty quickly. But once the graph is there, someone is bound to use AI to interpret it - opening that Pandora's box is inevitable. 

I take on board the points about scaling back some of the claims, and adding caveats around potential pitfalls, and I will redraft the CIP with this in mind. However, it is still my belief that this system can and will become equally, if not more trustworthy then traditional KYC. After all, you can buy a fake identity that will pass KYC on the darknet for a few hundred dollars - circumventing KYC is trivial to someone who knows what they're doing - it's one big single-point-of-failure. What would not be trivial, would be convincing a significant number of respected and established community members to literally stake some Ada on me as a person - sure, people can often be bought, but if it becomes apparent that a community member is consistently giving dodgy affirmations, that community member's trust rating can be expected to take a nose-dive. 

Or put more simply - I trust the community more than I trust the government - within the scheme I'm proposing, the government effectively becomes another member of the community, and it's up to the individual to decide how much weight they place on the government, versus their close circle, versus any factions they're a member of, versus the opinion of the wider community. 

The first step is building out the graph - ie, allowing people to give each other affirmations (I am very nearly ready to launch this). Initially I will not be deriving any trust ratings from it - I'm simply going to allow people to view their place on a network diagram. I anticipate that it will take some time for the graph to become established before it will be useful for actually determining trust scores, and there is no rush to do that - I won't start assigning trust scores until the graph is rich enough to contain useful information - it's better to do nothing than get it wrong!

Another possibility is to use the token itself as a stamp of validity: the token can only be stored in the UTxO if the UTxO is properly constructed. Then the indexers can just filter the current UTxO set by those that contain these tokens. Off-chain indexers make this very easy; they usually have dedicated "Asset UTxOs" endpoints ([maestro](https://docs.gomaestro.org/cardano/native-asset-utxos), [koios](https://preprod.koios.rest/#post-/asset_utxos)). This would provide more secure indexing than just using the affirmation address since it is possible to create invalid UTxOs at the address without executing the minting policy or staking script (ie, addresses can't deny UTxOs). It is quite old but the [beacon token CIP](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/pull/466) explains how to do this in a trustless setting; but if you think you can trust the UTxO creator, an adaptation of [CIP-68](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/tree/master/CIP-0068) may also work.

If a UTxO has a bunch of assets where one of them is a programmable token that needs this transfer script, this script can cause the entire UTxO to be stuck. A malicious person could possibly use this to attack Cardano where they deliberately trap a large number of UTxOs and all of their assets.

A UTxO in a user credential cannot have more than one smart token, so for instance a programmable stablecoin that gets frozen in your programmable token wallet cannot cause other programmable tokens to be frozen. However, at programmable token addresses derived from script credentials (ie. programmable token smart contract addresses), this is an unavoidable tradeoff of ERC-20 style programmable tokens. Imagine you have a smartUSD-smartYen liquidity pool, if the smartUSD `TransferLogicScript` returns false (ex. due to the issuer freezing the assets in that pool) then how would the pool continue to operate? If someone exchanges their lp tokens what should they get? In practice, it is the responsibility of dApp others to limit the amount of programmable tokens in each UTxO as much as possible (ideally a single programmable token per UTxO) but in pooled protocols, and other potential use-cases there will be times where multiple such assets will have to exist in the same UTxO and when that is the case the risks are as you described.

In this model, protocols like your P2P DeFi apps have a security advantage of natively not requiring multi-asset UTxOs by default, so I think protocols like yours are well suited for this design. In cases such as your lending/borrowing protocol, that behavior is simply unavoidable with programmable tokens which allow custodial management of the tokens, and this is exactly how programmability works in Ethereum / other blockchains which support it, if Circle freezes the USDC in a Uniswap pool, the pool is bricked, and all the users are essentially rugged. As a user in such pools, you have to be aware of the risks. Ideally you should never interact with programmable tokens that you do not trust as is the case in Ethereum.

The minUTxOValue incentivizes combining UTxOs as much as possible. Since there could easily be 100s of programmable tokens, I think it is unreasonable to expect users to dedicate each one to their own UTxO with a deposit of ~2 ADA per UTxO. Users are incentivized to deliberately switch to script based addresses just to get around this requirement.

> ... you should never interact with programmable tokens that you do not trust

It isn't enough to trust them. I really want to stress that a hack of the control for a programmable token could be a **systemic risk** to the entire blockchain. Imagine if there was an honest stablecoin issuer that was widely trusted and adopted, and they use a multisig to program the stablecoin. Since it is widely accepted, the stablecoin is *not* kept in separate UTxOs and is used across DeFi. If malicious actors get control of this multisig, they could effectively freeze a huge number of UTxOs and DeFi DApps across Cardano. Block production would be fine, but a huge number of UTxOs would become unspendable. This would be catastrophic and possibly cost $billions, if not $trillions, in damages.

As it is, we are trying to move away from the Genesis Keys because they are a central point of failure. Yet, with this CIP, a widely adopted programmable token effectively introduces new "critical keys".

All of these programmable token CIPs ultimately seem like [accidental complexity](https://javanexus.com/blog/navigating-accidental-essential-complexity) from not being able to properly model what we want with programmable tokens (ie, manage specific tokens but leave everything else alone). The eUTxO model isn't granular enough for this. I'd much prefer to see what L2s can do and have them absorb the risks over having L1 expose itself to the possible systemic risks. For example, there could be an L2 dedicated to royalties where the programming of the royalties for a specific NFT on L2 is controlled by an L1 token.

Hmm. This suggests that either the module resolution happens at compile time (which would void the benefits of having modules to begin with) or, actually done by the ledger itself executing scripts. So my understanding leans towards the later, which leads to the follow-up question: are you suggesting that the ledger becomes aware of scripts dependencies? And if so, by which means shall transaction communicate this intent to the ledger?

At the moment, scripts are fundamentally _already parameterized_ by a single parameter (two or three in PlutusV1 & PlutusV2); A validator has a signature that's roughly `Data -> Validator`. So I don't find it completely unreasonable to ask the ledger to now _also_ apply some dependencies to the scripts in addition to the datum/redeemer & script context. Though it's unclear at this point how to signal that and how is this being cost (will keep reading 👀).

I'd argue that it doesn't _eliminate_ the cost of evaluating scripts, but rather, it becomes someone's else problem 😄! That someone here being, the ledger/node indirectly which now has to do more (un-budgeted) work for free. I believe one of the fundamental design choice of Plutus was to have most of the decoding / conversion operations happen as part of the CEK evaluation so that they can be properly cost and paid for. 

Otherwise, I'd argue that instead of providing `Data` arguments to scripts, we might as well provide pre-computed sum-of-products. But that means the cost of decoding the script context is now not paid for by execution units so has to be acknowledged through different means.

(to be clear, I am not _against_ the idea! It seems like a reasonable ask to me, but I recall past conversations with the Plutus core team about it and why it is generally not deem as a viable option).

The exact same thing is true on Cardano. You can easily create proxy contracts that can be updated without changing its contract address. 

```haskell
mkProxyContract :: ClosedTerm (PAsData PCurrencySymbol :--> PScriptContext :--> PUnit)
mkProxyContract  = plam $ \protocolParamsCS ctx -> P.do
  ctxF <- pletFields @'["txInfo", "redeemer", "scriptInfo"] ctx
  infoF <- pletFields @'["inputs", "referenceInputs", "outputs", "signatories", "wdrl"] ctxF.txInfo

  referenceInputs <- plet $ pfromData infoF.referenceInputs

  -- Extract protocol parameter UTxO
  ptraceInfo "Extracting protocol parameter UTxO"
  let paramUTxO =
        pfield @"resolved" #$
          pmustFind @PBuiltinList
            # plam (\txIn ->
                    let resolvedIn = pfield @"resolved" # txIn
                    in phasDataCS # protocolParamsCS # (pfield @"value" # resolvedIn)
                  )
            # referenceInputs

  POutputDatum ((pfield @"outputDatum" #) -> paramDat') <- pmatch $ pfield @"datum" # paramUTxO
  forwardToScriptHash <- plet $ punsafeCoerce @_ @_ @(PAsData PByteString) (pto paramDat')

  let invokedScripts =
        pmap @PBuiltinList
          # plam (\wdrlPair ->
                    let cred = pfstBuiltin # wdrlPair
                    in punsafeCoerce @_ @_ @(PAsData PByteString) $ phead #$ psndBuiltin #$ pasConstr # pforgetData cred
                )
          # pto (pfromData infoF.wdrl)
  pif (pelem # forwardToScriptHash # invokedScripts) (pconstant ()) perror 
```

how can a contract manage keypairs on-chain and keep private key secret?

thanks for your interest.

would this work?

A contract alone typically cannot hold a private key “secret” on a fully transparent blockchain. Instead, one must use threshold cryptography or multi-party computation (MPC), where the key is split among multiple participants/nodes. Each piece is useless by itself, so no single party or on-chain entity has the entire private key. The contract effectively “manages” the key by coordinating partial signatures from these participants. Another approach is to store an encrypted key on-chain, and only decrypt it in a secure off-chain or MPC environment when the contract logic calls for a signature. In both cases, the actual private key bits are never revealed in plaintext on the public ledger.

(cBTC is a better name)

**Proposed Approach**

1. **Key Generation & Distribution**  
   - The bridging contract generates a Bitcoin key, then splits it into multiple fragments (e.g. via Shamir’s Secret Sharing).  
   - Each fragment is *encrypted* for a specific stake pool operator, using that operator’s on-chain public key.  
   - The contract publishes these encrypted fragments *on-chain*, so nobody sees the raw private key.

2. **Minting cBTC**  
   - User deposits BTC to a 2-of-2 address (part user key, part bridging key).  
   - A proof (e.g. NiPoPoW) is submitted to the bridging contract.  
   - The contract “mints” cBTC tokens on Cardano for that user, representing the locked BTC.  

3. **Burn-to-Release Process**  
   - To unlock the BTC back on Bitcoin, the user *burns* their cBTC on Cardano.  
   - The contract detects this burn event and proceeds to *reassemble* its share of the private key.  

4. **Recombining Key Fragments**  
   - Each stake pool operator retrieves *its own* encrypted fragment from the chain, decrypts it locally (with its private key), and provides a *partial* signature or partial decryption to the contract.  
   - Once the threshold (e.g. t-of-n stake pools) has cooperated, the contract can reconstruct its share of the BTC key *on-chain*.  

5. **Completing the BTC Spend**  
   - The contract then co-signs (with the user’s key) a transaction that releases BTC to the user’s chosen address on Bitcoin.  
   - This happens automatically as soon as enough stake pool operators submit valid partial decryptions.

**Why It’s Trustless & Automated**  
- No single stake pool operator or the contract itself holds the entire private key; collusion of *at least t* is required.  
- The bridging contract enforces “burn cBTC first” before releasing key material to sign the BTC transaction.  
- Stake pools already run infrastructure for Cardano, so they can securely manage key fragments in a similar automated fashion.  
- Everything from fragment distribution to partial-sig aggregation is orchestrated by the contract, *on-chain*, ensuring transparency and preventing unauthorized BTC spends.

I was not sure about this, so additional info:

**How the User Gets a Deposit Address & Provides a NiPoPoW**

1. **Contract Generates Address**  
   - First, the user calls the bridging contract on Cardano asking for a unique deposit address on Bitcoin (e.g., a 2-of-2 multi-sig address).  
   - The contract creates this address by combining the user’s public key with the contract’s bridging key.

2. **User Deposits BTC**  
   - The user sends BTC to that newly generated address.  
   - Once enough confirmations have passed, the user (or any off-chain service) can gather a NiPoPoW (Non-Interactive Proof of Proof-of-Work) that proves “X BTC was deposited to that address.”

3. **User Submits NiPoPoW**  
   - The user returns to the Cardano contract and submits the NiPoPoW proof, indicating the transaction ID, the address, and the confirmed deposit.  
   - The bridging contract verifies the proof on-chain to confirm the BTC is locked at the multi-sig address.

4. **Contract Mints cBTC**  
   - After successful verification, the contract mints the corresponding amount of “cBTC” for the user on Cardano.  

Thus, the user *first* obtains a fresh deposit address (step 1), sends BTC to it (step 2), then uses NiPoPoW (steps 3–4) to prove that deposit to the bridging contract—no trust in a single custodian required.

Equivocating blocks must *not* be discarded, this would lead to an unsound protocol (e.g. the adversary could relatively easily cause a network partition by diffusing different equivocating forks to different parts of the network, and letting two chains grow on top of them). I think it makes sense to just remove this part; handling of equivocating blocks isn't really related to Peras.

The researchers currently assume that equivocating certificates is impossible, so this case can probably be removed (and instead this assumption can be stated upfront).

If one simply discards equivocating votes, then honest nodes might disagree forever in whether they have seen a certificate for a round (the idea again is for the adversary to diffuse equivocating votes to different people). One way around this here that seems realistic for the actual implementation is to diffuse certificates between caught-up nodes in this case.

The constraint $L\leq U$ seems unnecessary; the statement

> Rule VR-1B will fail if the candidate block is older than the most recently certified block.

seems to try to justify it, but the most recently certified block (so usually the one certified in the previous round) will also be a block older than $L$ than the start of the previous round, so there should be no problem per se in having $L>U$ AFAICT.
Maybe instead link to e.g. https://github.com/input-output-hk/peras-design/pull/247?

This low value for $L$ (due to the lack of pre-agreement) allows relatively weak adversaries (e.g. weaker than 25%) to induce frequent cooldowns due to "vote splitting attacks", ie the adversary has a short fork with a different block $L$ slots before the start of a round, and then diffuses just barely before the round starts to (see "Honest vote splitting", in particular Figure A.1 in https://tweag.github.io/cardano-peras/peras-design.pdf for more details and concrete numbers), such that the honest vote is split and no quorum is reached.

One can make things a bit better by choosing a larger $L$, but it doesn't actually help much (or rather, one would have to make $L$ so large as for Peras to become much less useful).

I think it is enough to just point out somewhere in the CIP that one has to accept this downside for pre-alpha Peras.

How were these chosen? We have

 - $A = T_{\text{heal}} + T_{\text{CQ}}$, 
 - $R = \lceil A/U \rceil$ and 
 - $K = \lceil (A + T_{\text{CP}}) / U \rceil$. 

From the Praos mainnet parameterization (see e.g. [here](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1B8BNMx8jVWRjYiUBOaI3jfZ7dQNvNTSDODvT5iOuYCU/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.qh2zcajmu6hm)), we have $T_{\text{CQ}} = k/f = 43200$ and $T_{\text{CP}} = 3k/f = 129600$, so we get

 - $A \ge 43200$,
 - $R \ge 480$,
 - $K \ge 1920$

for $U=90$. These values are already much larger than the ones listed here, and they do not yet account for $T_{\text{heal}}$.

One thing to mention here is that we can't seem to be able to prevent adversaries from including useless certificates on chain when Peras is *not* in a cooldown (also see "Changes to the Ledger " in https://tweag.github.io/cardano-peras/peras-design.pdf for more details).

```haskell
data Tx = Tx
  { body :: TxBody
  , wits :: TxWits
  , auxData :: Maybe AuxData
  , isValid :: Bool
  }
data TxBody = TxBody
  { inputs :: [TxIn]

data SubTx = Tx
  { body :: TxBody
  , wits :: TxWits
  , auxData :: Maybe AuxData
  }
```
Note that SubTx does not have the isValid flag, because it would not make sense for an individual subtransaction to indicate that information.

```haskell
tx =
  Body
  { inputs = [txIn0:FOO 5]
  , outputs = [txOut:ADA 5]
  , fee = 5 ADA
  , subTx =
     [ Tx
       { body = Body
         { inputs = [txIn00:FOO 95]
         , outpus = [txOut00:ADA 200]
         , requiredObservers = [scriptHash00]
         }
       , wits = Wits
         { redeemers = [ (RedeemerPtr ReqObserver 0, (_exUnits000, data000))
                       , (RedeemerPtr Spending 0, (exUnits001, data001))
                       ]
         }
       }
     , Tx
       { body = Body
         { inputs = [txIn10:ADA 210]
         , outpus = [txOut10:FOO 100]
         , requiredObservers = [scriptHash10]
         }
       , wits = Wits
         { redeemers = [ (RedeemerPtr ReqObserver 0, (_exUnits100, data100))
                       ]
         }
       }
     ]
  , observers = [scriptHash0]
  }
  Wits {
   redeemers = [ (RedeemerPtr ReqObservers (0, 0)), (exUnits00, data00)
               , (RedeemerPtr ReqObservers (1, 0)), (exUnits10, data10)
               , (RedeemerPtr Spending 0, (exUnits0, data0))
               ]
  }
```
This is a nice example, since it captures couple of different uses cases:
* performing a swap 
* top level transaction builder is paying the fee with a multi asset (aka Babel fee)
* execution of scripts at all levels

So, if you look at the redeemers for the top level transaction there are three of them. Which means at the top level three independent script executions will occur and all of them will have the same `TxInfo`, which will contain all of the sub transactions.

Spending scripts, on the other hand, that specified in the subtransactions will have access only to their own TxInfo.
Note:
* that the underscore in `_exUnits000` and `_exUnits100`, it indicates those execution units have to be ignored, for obvious reasons.
* Both top level and sub transactions will have ability to supply data, eg, `scriptHash00` will receive both `data000` and `data00` as arguments. This will be a nice mechanism for top level transaction to communicate with the sub transaction  programmatically. Naturally `data00` could be ignored by the script, if it is not suppose to be used.

@bezirg In some ways, yes it allows that, but primarily, the purpose is very similar to this script. It just allows you to define a function `f` in one script and call it in a different script. 

The reason the docs talk about memorization, is because many of the popular use-cases of this design pattern allow the user the option to write the result of `f` to the chain, such that the next time a script uses merkelized validators to call `f` on a given value (that has already been executed before) the transaction does not need to actually evaluate `f` anymore. When you opt to memorize a given execution, the result of `f` on the given argument is stored with an NFT in a script. Subsequent calls of `f` on that specific argument `arg`, can simply provide the UTxO with that NFT as a reference input and read the result of `(f arg)` from the datum of that reference input, instead of redundantly executing `(f arg)` again since the value is already known as it has already been computed in a previous transaction.

I agree that a `BuiltinMaryEraValue` type would be preferable, but it would only be preferable if we can guarantee that we can have the values in script context all have this type when this `BuiltinMaryEraValue` is implemented. I opted for the `BuiltinData` definition because one of the issues I remember from the `BuiltinArray` discussion is that even if we get `BuiltinArray` the relevant script context fields will still be encoded as `BuiltinList` and we would need to use a builtin to first convert them to `BuiltinArray`. Importantly, both `MintValue` and `Value` obey all the invariants I described above. I deliberately excluded the additional invariant "Every non-empty map must contain an entry for Ada, and the first key of any non-empty map must correspond to that Ada entry", I also excluded "all quantities must be positive` for similar reasons (and importantly for allowing subtracting values by unioning values with values that are negations of what you want to subtract). 

Both `MintValue` and `Value` will be represented by the `BuiltinMaryEraValue` builtin, in the same way that right now, they are both represented as newtypes around `BuiltinMap (BI.BuiltinList (BI.BuiltinPair BI.BuiltinData BI.BuiltinData))`. 

The only reason `MintValue` was introduced in the first place was because we needed a way at the type level to convey the difference in invariants between `Value` and `MintValue` and to discourage the use of certain operations on `MintValue` (a result of issues I raised with how some of the standard library value operations interacted with `MintValue`). When we introduce `BuiltinMaryEraValue`, this will not change. They will both have different newtypes which convey the difference in invariants to developers and expose operations accordingly.

The invariants of `BuiltinMaryEraValue` should not be all the invariants of the different values in the script context, instead they should be only those which must always be preserved across any operation on values. There is no benefit to having the `BuiltinMaryEraValue` impose invariants like `must contain ada` or `must not contain negative quantities of tokens`, because operations across values can break those invariants and then the result would not be representable by `BuiltinMaryEraValue`. If you union a value that contains only 10 ada with a value that contains only negative -10 ada the result should be an empty value. If you use the `deleteCoin` builtin to remove Ada from a `BuiltinMaryEraValue` the result should still be a `BuiltinMaryEraValue` (this is an extremely common use-case, ie you have some UTxO that only contains an minAda and NFT and you want the script to confirm the continuing output always must contain that NFT but allow the ada to change so that the script doesn't break from a protocol parameters update to Cardano, then you do `deleteCoin adaCS adaTokenName ownInputValue == deleteCoin adaCS adaTokenName ownOutputValue`).

>we introduced MintValue quite late, do you think that there are other kinds of "Value" which will need introducing? Is this specification of Value stable across multiple kinds of "Value"?

Yes, this specification is suitable for every type of value that currently exists, and any reasonable type of value that would exist in the future. The only way this would ever become unsuitable is if there is a fundamental change to the multi-asset model of the ledger, which is so deeply engrained into the code-base and architecture of Cardano at this point that such a change would never ever be considered.

I have never seen a production use-case that does any order comparison other than `valueEq`, `valueLessThan` or `valueGreaterThan` all of which can be easily expressed by `valueContains` and data equality on `BuiltinMaryEraValue`. Similarly, `checkBin` exists in Plutarch's standard library as-well, and there is not a single instance of it being used outside of to implement the order comparisons that I mentioned above. 

Not only is there no real use-case for `checkBin` but also implementing it as a builtin would be very difficult to cost and requires something akin to limited higher order functions which we will not get in PlutusCore for a very long time. I believe this just adds a ton of complexity with no real use-case. The only case I could see this being useful is if you want to check that a value is X amount greater than another value, but for this to be possible we need limited higher order builtins, and so I propose if this is something we want, we just propose this as an additional builtin down the line once we have limited higher order builtins implemented and leave it out of scope for this CIP.

[More of a historical note than a relevant comment...]  I think it was a deliberate decision to make UPLC as general as possible so as not to unduly restrict the capabilities of on-chain code, and UPLC was designed very early on, before we even know what sort of scripts people would want to write.  For instance UPLC had been in existence for a year or two before the `Value` type took its final form, and similarly for the general EUTXO model, whose design was inspired by experiments involving things written in PlutusTx/Plinth.  I think also that it was initially believed that Scott encoding could be used to represent any kind of data structure that might be required on the chain, and it was only considerably later that it turned out that that wasn't feasible because of the constraints imposed on scripts by on-chain resource limits (the node and the network were evolving in parallel with the UPLC language so these constraints weren't known in advance).  

I think there was a bit of a chicken and egg problem: without a language, people couldn't write scripts, and without people writing scripts we didn't know what sort of things they'd want to do with the language.  As you point out, `Value` has turned out to be very important so it would be good to be able to deal with it efficiently, so your proposal is very welcome.

With the benefit of hindsight we could design a low-level language better suited to the purposes of the chain than UPLC is.  That might even be possible, since I believe that the ledger is agnostic about the language that scripts are written in and could potentially support different evaluators for different languages.  It would be a major effort to design such a new language and safely integrate it with the chain though, so I don't think that's likely to happen any time soon.
I don't think you actually say what a `Coin` is anywhere.  Presumably it's a `currency symbol, token name, quantity)` triple, but it would be worth saying that expicitly.

The second option seems more sensible since if the `Value` type is something opaque then all of the operations can be designed to preserve the invariants, although you'll need some `Data -> Value` function (and its inverse) which checks for well-formedness when it's doing the conversion; once you've got a `Value` object though, you can do what you want and be confident that it'll  remain well-formed.  Also, if we use some specialised type it could be made more efficient than the current list-based format used in `Data`.

If you just use `Data`, though, you'll in general have no guarantee that a supposed `Value` object satisfies the invariants, or even that it doesn't contain irrelevant types of `Data` subobjects, like pairs.  That would suggest that all of the operations would have to check that their arguments are well-formed, which might add a lot of overhead.  Maybe we could supply a single function to check that a `Data` object is a well-formed `Value` and make the other functions less strict about checking, but then the overhead might be similar to converting to an opaque `Value` type.

The costing issue is an important one, and it might influence the design of the type and the functions operating on it.  We have to assign a costing function to each new builtin, and before a function is applied to some `Value` (`v`, say), we have to measure the size of `v` and estimate the CPU and memory costs of the function based on that size, and only proceed if there's sufficient budget left to pay those costs.  The nested structure of the `Value` type makes this very tricky.  Suppose you're using lists of pairs to implement maps, so `Value` would be something like (in Haskell notation) `[(CurrencySymbol, [(TokenName, Integer)])]`. If you want to look up the quantity `q` of token `t` for currency `c` , you first of all have to find `c` in the outer list, and you can work  out the potential cost of this by looking at the length of the list; however, you can't tell how long it'll take to find `t` in the inner list until you've found `c` in the outer list, so you'd have to do most of the work of looking up `q` in order to work out how much it'll cost to look it up, which kind of defeats the purpose.  I think this will need more thought, and we'll defintely need to take it into consideration when designing the functions.  One thing we could do would be to flatten the whole thing out and have a map of `(c,t)` pairs to quantities (so the cost would only depend on the number of such pairs), but would  it be possible to do this efficiently while still maintaining the invariants?   Maybe a Haskell `Data.Map` would be  suitable for this, in particular because it can tell you in constant time how big it is.  I haven't thought this through though, so it may well not be sensible.

Anoother factor that might influence the design is what typical `Values` on the chain look like.  We could use some complex tree-based type, but if 99% of the `Values` on the chain have only 5 entries that it might be easier (and in fact more efficient) to just use lists.  I've just remembered that I analysed all of the scripts on the chain and looked at the structure of the `Values` they used: the results are described  [here](https://github.com/IntersectMBO/plutus/blob/master/plutus-ledger-api/exe/analyse-script-events/Values.md#values-appearing-in-transaction-outputs), and in fact most of them were pretty small. That was 18  months ago though, so it might be worth repeating the exercise.  Also, who can tell what might happen in the future?  If we implement something based on small numbers of tokens and then in a few years there are scripts that manipulate millions of them then it might be problematic.

Something else to worry about is how these things will be serialised.  If scripts are allowed to contain literal `Value`s then we have to  consider how they're converted into the `flat` format that gets used for serialised scripts. If you have enormous values in scripts then possibly the deserialisation cost could become large enough to be problematic. Maybe this isn't an issue, but we should think about it.  Perhaps we could prohibit serialisation of whatever internal format we end up using for `Value`s and require them to be serialised as `data` and then explicitly converted to `Value` during script execution with the conversion cost being paid for as normal rather than being done for free when the node deserialises scripts.
