It is not an issue of wording. I believe it as in issue of confusing two different features. We have a [CIP-112 Observer type](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/pull/749) that specifically designed to deal with top level scripts that run once for the whole transaction. Which would match the semantics of what you are talking about: "single execution"

In this case we need for sub-transaction to be able to specify arguments to a script that will run at a top level. Which means if two separate sub-transactions specify the same script but two different arguments, you cannot run the script "once", you need to run it as many times as it appears in all of the subtransactions with different arguments. This is a crucial feature for nested transactions, because there would be no other way for sub transaction builder to run and influence the outcome of script at the top level that is unique to that sub-transaction.

It is akin to saying "these two certificates are locked by the same script, we should be able to run that script only once". Which, naturally is not the case, because they will have different arguments and different execution units, hence will be executed multiple times. Same concept will be applied to required observers for sub-transactions.

So there's a design space here, and the question is how to deal with multiple subtransactions requiring the same observer. The observer could either run once in total or once per subtransaction that requires it, both of these are valid options. So the question becomes which design is preferred here.

One reason why it seems more natural to me to have a single execution of the script is that subtransactions cannot provide a redeemer in the current design, since it wouldn't be signed. So all redeemers would have to be provided at the top level transaction, but then you could just simplify this to a single execution anyway. That has the benefit of better performance which is nice.

So, the question becomes: is there a use case for multiple executions of a batch observer that makes it worth the extra effort of adding signed redeemers? Since we're probably adding regular observers as well, I don't think consistency with other script purposes is really an argument here anymore.

I don't know which option @polinavino originally had in mind here, but with the way CIP is currently designed single execution seems more natural.

> One reason why it seems more natural to me to have a single execution of the script is that subtransactions cannot provide a redeemer in the current design, since it wouldn't be signed. So all redeemers would have to be provided at the top level transaction, but then you could just simplify this to a single execution anyway.

This is actually incorrect. Sub transaction will be supplying redeemers and will be signing them, all like with a regular transaction, except for the observers that they require to be executed at the top level since they can't possibly know the amount of execution units that will be required for running such script.

> So, the question becomes: is there a use case for multiple executions of a batch observer that makes it worth the extra effort of adding signed redeemers?

The answer is: it is a requirement. Not for all cases, but without ability of a sub-transaction builder to supply an argument to a script it has no way of affecting the outcome of execution of such script, unless the author hard codes the values, in which case such script cannot be shared with any other sub-transaction anyways.

I have talked to Ziyang about this and he is 100% agreement with me that without ability to provide arguments to a script this feature is practically useless. So, having nice performance isn't very useful if a feature is useless.

In any case. I believe I have a solution that would allow the user to choose which approach suites their use case best. It requires CIP-112, which we were planning to implement anyways for the next era.

We add to the sub transaction body a list of `ReqObservers`:
```haskell
data ReqObserver = ReqObserver
    { reqObserver :: !(Credential 'Observer)
    -- ^ Key hash, or script hash of a plutus or native script
    , reqScriptData :: !(Maybe Data)
    -- ^ In case of a native script or a key hash it is a failure to supply this argument. In case of
    -- a plutus script this is an optional argument. If data is supplied for a plutus script then it
    -- will be executed as `SubTxObserverPurpose` otherwise it will have to be included 
    -- in the `reqObservers` of top level transaction, by the top level Tx builder
    }
```

In other words if a user specifies an argument to a script then it will be a unique execution regardless if other sub-transactions use the same script, but if the argument is not supplied then such script will have to be placed into requiredObservers at the top level, which will lead to de-duplication of execution if other sub-transaction use the same script also without supplying arguments.

Redundant script executions are a massive burden on the ledger. The vast majority of ex-budget consumed onchain up to this point is entirely from completely redundant validation. We need to limit this to preserve room for meaningful computation. 

To address your concern of an input script needing to redundantly check for outputs, we can introduce two purposes for Guarding scripts. The `GuardingPurpose` will be invoked if there is a UTxO output to the script and no UTxO is spent from the script. The `GuardingContinuingPurpose ScriptHash` will be invoked if there is both a UTxO spent from the script, and a UTxO output to the script. That way if you are simply spending a UTxO from the script you can safely avoid checking for any outputs to the script.

@fallen-icarus ToCs are neither standard nor non-standard in CIPs.  They are rare _in Markdown_ because the outline structure is so easily parseable from the raw text and because the section deep links are generated automatically which simplifies point-to-point linking within the document itself.

They are only regular in _CIP *sections*_ when a section is so detailed it needs heading navigation.  For instance, when you're in a complex _Specification_ you may need to easily jump to other parts of that specification; most famously here: https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/blob/master/CIP-1694/README.md#specification

Editors have always removed / repositioned sections inserted before the _Abstract_ since Day 1 of the CIP process.  Besides the standard & familiar YAML header, it's one of the things that make CIPs look like CIPs and therefore provides a continuity of reading experience across the document repository.

If you still would like a combined ToC that spans both the _Motivation_ and _Specification_, you could move your unabridged ToC to the end of the document (where we have agreed to house _[optional sections](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/blob/master/CIP-0001/README.md#structure)_) and then link to it from your Abstract.  (The gimmick of accordioning it into the Abstract section likely would break something someday because abstracts are generally quoted in other digests, papers & directories.)

It seems to me that you and I are talking about different consumers of ToCs. You are talking about machines parsing them and I am talking about humans reading them. ToCs serve as an outline for what is to follow. Jumping around the page is a second use case. (I frequently skim ToCs of books when deciding what to read.)

Both [BIPs](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0032.mediawiki) and [EIPs](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-100) have ToCs at the top. IMHO I think CIPs should have them too because starting with the outline makes CIPs more approachable.

No, we're talking about the difference between a human reading 1 CIP and a human reading a lot of them.  I don't just mean the editors: we're thinking of implementors, looking for the CIP that matches what they are doing, plus others who are reading through multiple CIPs with the same level of interest.

From this level, what a CIP is about is more important than the particulars that are in it — or at least _more general_ — and therefore the Abstract needs to go at the top.  Having the ToC at the top suits the arrivals who already know what a CIP is about: while we are trying to facilitate new arrivals and adopters.  CIPs were conceived in this ethos, which was also supported in their remodel a couple years later in adding "why is this CIP necessary?" and "how does this CIP achieve its goals?" to _Motivation_ and _Rationale_.

@lehins that 3% APY was a compromise between the previous 8% yield from early the Shelley Era which has been compounding for longer, and also with the expectation that future things will be done to increase rewards such as Partner Chain AVS.  If the community does nothing to increase rewards, then the model has the estimate around 0.6% APY by 2030, which is likely unsustainable and another problem entirely.

SPO retirement does indeed remove stake from circulation, but an SPO with large amounts of immobile, lost stake is incentivized NOT to retire.  Even if their performance is poor or they are acting maliciously, by definition that stake will stay with them.  Additionally, with the model's projections it is likely that the problem will be quite bad within the lifetime of a single human who operates a stake pool.  And even then there's the possibility/likelihood of it being passed on.

As far as other methods of estimating or projecting lost stake, we also looked at...
- Residual stake left in pools after they retire
- Counting rewards (account) balances in wallets that have not had activity in X amount of time.
- Counting eligible wallets that don't claim their $NIGHT airdrop

The issue is that each of those things is a lot of extra, uncompensated work and at best they are only rough estimates as well.  We think it is more important to at least conclude that the problem exists even if we can't quantify the magnitude of it.

I do think our biggest saving grace for this problem is the existence of a saturation cap on each pool that sets on upper limit on lost rewards compounding infinitely.  But that is also very hard to estimate or model without a way to actually identify lost stake on chain.

It is similar but not identical to Mithril: one of the signatures in the certificate is an ordinary BLS multisig, but the second aggregate signature attests to the right to vote. I've attached the mathematical details from the original Leios paper. The [Certificate](https://github.com/cardano-scaling/CIPs/blob/leios/CIP-%3F%3F%3F%3F/README.md#votes-certificates-cddl) contains a record of the voters included in the certificate: see `persistent_voters` and `nonpersistent_voters` in the CDDL below. Each node has the public keys of all stakepools from the previous key registrations and the list of persistent voters for the epoch is computed prior to the start of the epoch. The local tally may be different among nodes and nodes need not have seen any votes at all, but they can verify the certificate because the certificate itself contains the BLS signatures of the non-persistent voters and a record of which persistent voters actually voted. ```cddl leios_certificate = [ election_id : election_id , endorser_block_hash : hash32 , persistent_voters : [* persistent_voter_id] , nonpersistent_voters : {* pool_id => bls_signature} , ? aggregate_elig_sig : bls_signature , aggregate_vote_sig : bls_signature ] ``` The [`verify_cert`](https://github.com/input-output-hk/ouroboros-leios/blob/42efc920cbd1acc01793953a5fc2b4b9bd225028/crypto-benchmarks.rs/src/cert.rs#L116) function in the prototype implementation of the cryptography provides a concrete realization where a certificate is verified from previously registered information. @rrtoledo may want to comment and clarify further.

Here are the assumptions:

1. It assumes that (in the aggregate), SPOs were approximately profitable when the price was 0.75 USD/ADA. This is based on anecdotal evidence, since there is no comprehensive survey of SPO profitability and SPOs have widely varying infrastructure costs.
2. Analysis of recent `mainnet` data indicates that approximately 21% of all rewards accrue to SPOs, with the remaining 79% accruing to individual wallets.
3. Recent `mainnet` history also suggests that fees accumulate at the rate of 0.34 ADA per transaction.
4. On a per-epoch basis, approximately 1.6M ADA in rewards is distributed to SPOs.
5. During that time the observed throughput of `mainnet` was 0.6 transactions/second.

The "break even" assumption `(1)` allows us to estimate ***expenses*** from the SPO rewards `(4`), the TPS at the break-even point `(5)`, and the fee rate `(3)`. We chose to plot the ratio of revenues to expenses rather than their absolute values in order to avoid distractions and so the "break even" line is a 100% ratio by construction. The "business as usual" assumption is important here, since the fees from transactions (due to size and Plutus) and the number and hosting of SPOs may change in the future.

Needless to say, this is a very approximate analyses but, sadly, an precise estimate is not possible without access to SPO financials. However, one of the goals of this proposal was to simplify the design in an effort to reduce development time. Towards this end, we made the assumption that  any certified EB will be delivered sufficiently fast so that it won't delay the adoption of any RB whose validity depends on the EB. This allowed us to minimize the impact of the proposal to other actors in the Cardano ecosystem, e.g., light clients.

Now, given that such an RB (whose validity depends on an EB) can be produced quite fast (after about 3 L_hdr + L_vote + L_diff slots), increasing the voting threshold (e.g., to 75%) allows us to ensure better diffusion of the EB. Concretely, if the threshold is at x%, and we are up against an attacker controlling 49% of the network, then a certified EB is guaranteed to have been seen and processed by (x-49)% of the stake by the end of L_vote. When x:=51%, x-49 is 2. When x:=75%, x-49 ~26.  Given the large size of EBs, 2% may be insufficient for quick delivery of EBs.

Concluding,  increasing the voting threshold can help us boost EB diffusion guarantees. Identifying where exactly the threshold should be to ensure timely diffusion of EBs should be further studied in the next phase of development. Finally, note that future versions of the protocol are expected to be less sensitive to the threshold level, as the burden of carrying data will move from EBs to IBs (as in the paper) and EB size will shrink.

```suggestion
The lost-stake problem is the accumulation of this unreachable-yet-delegated ADA within the Cardano ecosystem. Such lost stake still contributes to stake-pool sizes and earns staking rewards every epoch, even though the rewards accumulate in an address that nobody controls. For as long as the chosen stake pool produces staking rewards, the lost ADA compounds. Rewards paid to these addresses increase their delegated stake, which in turn earns more rewards, and so on. Similarly, if the lost ADA was delegated to a governance representative (dRep) for Voltaire-era on-chain voting, that voting power remains with the dRep permanently (or until the dRep retires or is marked inactive). The original owner is no longer present to adjust their delegation in response to changing conditions. This creates a class of delegation that cannot be reallocated or corrected.
```

I suggested including this field. My primary motivation was indirect: all of the logic in the existing Praos mini protocols maintains an invariant that requires this field. That invariant is as follows.

> Whenever the node is deciding what to request next and which peer to request it from, the size of what is being requested influences that decision logic.

There are two aspects of EBs that mean this `tx_size` field is required in order to enable that same invariant for the EB fetch decision logic.

- EBs are potentially quite large. This means we do need EB fetch logic; we can't simply request every EB from every peer (like we do with RB headers, for example). But they're not all the same size; some could be 100s of times smaller than others.
- EBs contain tx references instead of the txs themselves so that nodes can request a subset of the txs when they already have some (hopefully most!) of the txs that the desired EB references.

---

That's the motivation for `tx_size` so far. How does that sit with you?

Disclaimer: I don't know any _inescapable_ reasons why we have this invariant the first place. It certainly seems like a reasonable invariant to have---and so I wanted the CIP Leios to continue to enable it---but I think someone else would have to spell out why it's an invariant of the Cardano Diffusion Layer's design.

```suggestion
The core principle of the proposed protocol change is to **substantially escalate the computational cost of each grinding attempt for an adversary**. To achieve this, every honest participant is required to perform a designated computation for each block they produce over an epoch (**432,000 slots - 5 days**) - note that this computation can be preprocessed locally at the beginning of the epoch. Consequently, an adversary attempting a grinding attack must **recompute these operations for every single attempt**, while being **constrained by the grinding window**, which dramatically increases the resource expenditure. By enforcing this computational burden, we **drastically reduce the feasible number of grinding attempts** an adversary with a fixed resource budget can execute, making randomness manipulation **more expensive and significantly less practical**.
```

> Same applies to all of the witnesses. You don't need scripts or redeemers or signatures if you just want to reconstruct the ledger state.

> You cannot download just bodies and validate them with respect to the ledger! You either need a full transaction or you don't do any validation. You can't just be picking and choosing what you want to validate.

This is not true. Scripts, Witnesses, and redeemers are fundamentally different with regards to the validity and trust assumptions compared to the auxilary data like transaction metadata.

If I don't ever need to look at the auxiliary metadata, and never depend on it for business logic, then I can get a fully trustless node by validating block headers and the transaction body + witness set. Regardless of what the preimage was, someone can't present me with fallacious data, because I'm not downloading the preimage, and consensus doesn't consider the auxiliary data for selecting a chain.

On the other hand, if I avoid downloading the witness set, then I have a fundamentally different trust model; I don't know the redeemers to apply to the scripts to even run them; I don't know whether the transaction is even authorized to spend the UTxOs.

There are ends of a spectrum, of course: I can have a trust-full node by ignoring the witness set, of course, and at the end of the day a full node needs to download the auxiliary data to make it available, I'm not arguing that that spectrum doesn't exist.

But I still maintain that there is a fundamental difference between these things; the body lets you trust-fully reproduce the ledger state; the block headers + tx bodies + witnesses let you trust-lessly validate and reproduce the ledger state; the block headers + tx bodies + witness + auxiliary data lets you fully replicate and serve all historical state, including non-ledger state like transaction metadata.

Again, I'm just sharing this as another point of data for what I thought someone had told me the motivation was, in case that shook forth additional context / memories / motivation for the people like yourself; I may certainly be misremembering, and I quite agree that it's likely not very relevant in todays landscape.

We discussed some of your questions during the call earlier today, so I'll be a little brief in the responses. Please feel free to (re-)object to parts of my explanation here that seem dissatisfying.

> I assume that we're also separating the notion of a node's current chain from the notion of what prefix of the node's chain has a ledger computed for it. With the idea that we can quickly validate and select an alternative fork, without having to compute the ledger for that fork.

> The bit that seems problematic to me is the idea that we receive all EBs from competing forks. At a minimum, it's unclear what this really means and how that could be implemented given the existing Praos protocols (which apparently are not intended to be changed).

> And how with the existing protocols? A node only sees one upstream chain for each peer at once. So "all" forks are not visible to all nodes. Worse forks are inherently pruned in the relaying process by selecting only the best chain at each hop.

The key point that this question brings to mind for me is that MsgLeiosBlockAnnouncement sends the RB header independently of ChainSync and moreover independently of chains. Only opcert issue numbers are influenced by recent headers, so the client receiving MsgLeiosBlockAnnouncement doesn't even need to have received the preceding header. (There're more details written about the consequences of the missing opcert issue numbers elsewhere.)

> What does it really mean? Any valid fork (within the last K) blocks? For example, if I (as an adversary) make 1-block extensions of old nodes, do I expect every other node in the network to go back and fetch an EB for that fork just in case this chain could become a longest/densest chain? Surely not. That sounds like a DoS attack.

The intended idea is that the node will have acquired _every_ EB as they arise, even if those EBs are not on the node's current chain. And the conservative rule is for it would retain those EB until the node's immutable tip's slot implies the node could never select a chain that includes that EB.

A key factor is that the Leios anti-equivocation mechanisms prevent the node from ever downloading more than one EB per Praos election (or maybe it's 2). I don't remember the exact math, but the ballpark number from the last time Esgen walked me through the appropriate probability bounds was that even with grinding there couldn't be more than ~11,000 elections per 36 hours on `mainnet`. 12.5 megabytes * 2 * 11,000 is 275 gigabytes, which is frighteningly large but also isn't completely intractable worst-case. And a less conservative rule (eg 6 hrs/not assuming grinding/etc) might be justifiable.

> And in general it's not possible to see alternative forks early, and thus not possible to see EBs early. If we have a temporary 2-way network split, then by definition, nodes in each partition cannot see the chain(s) from the other partition. If those partitions are re-connected within K blocks then at that moment, the chains become visible, but the EBs will necessarily have to be fetched at this point. They cannot be fetched earlier.

Partitions do pose a challenge. If they're very lopsided, then the big side could be producing certs and the small side would be forced to fetch the EBs once the partition ends and could not contribute until it finishes catching-up. If the partition is more so balanced such that no side is "big", then there are no certs, and so there will never be a need for either side to recover the EBs they missed out on when the partition ends. The fact that the adversary can be fully present in multiple sides of a partition does complicate those claims a bit, but with a cert threshold of 75%, the adversary would have to have 50% stake in order to cause multiple sides of a perfect-storm partition to create certs.

The optimistic perspective can be summarized by noting that only the small side(s) of a partition would be delayed recovering EBs that the big side of a partition was able to certify during the partition. The small side grows its chain more slowly since it's the small side, so the partition would have to last for quite some time before that side risked having it's own 2161st block. Even the delay of having to fetch however many EBs is likely a small fraction of the duration of a partition that would introduce the risk of the small side growing its own 2161st block (unless the adversary was also issuing blocks on that side's chain with its full, say, 40% stake).

## Why Linear Leios?

I am opening this thread to have a more scoped discussion on specific issues that have been raised by reviewers, particularly by @dcoutts in his [latest review](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/pull/1078#issuecomment-3389327236).  
Thank you for taking the time to share such a thoughtful and detailed perspective.

Also thanks to @fallen-icarus <sup>[1](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/pull/1078#issuecomment-3390177857)</sup> and @mpizenberg <sup>[2](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/pull/1078#issuecomment-3394280488)</sup> for adding valuable insights to this discussion.

### Throughput and Performance Considerations

> “...we (i.e. the community) still will want full Leios because 100 TPS is great as an intermediate level of performance, but not enough for the long term.”

While this reflects a valid concern raised by @dcoutts in his capacity as a TSC member, the 100 TPS figure appears to be a conservative estimate rather than a fixed community consensus.
Based on simulations, the upper bound for Linear Leios is closer to **300 TxkB/s**, which depending on average transaction size, is substantially higher than 100 TPS:

| Avg Tx Size (bytes) | TPS @ 50 Tx kB/s | TPS @ 100 Tx kB/s | TPS @ 200 Tx kB/s | TPS @ 300 Tx kB/s |
|----------------------|------------------|-------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| 300 B   | 166.7 | 333.3 | 666.7 | **1 000** |
| 500 B   | 100 | 200 | 400 | **600** |
| 800 B   | 62.5 | 125 | 250 | **375** |
| 1 000 B | 50 | 100 | 200 | **300** |
| 1 200 B | 41.7 | 83.3 | 166.7 | **250** |
| 1 600 B | 31.3 | 62.5 | 125 | **187.5** |

This performance comfortably exceeds current network needs and achieves economic sustainability, as shown in [Figure 2](https://github.com/cardano-scaling/CIPs/blob/leios/CIP-0164/README.md#figure-2) of the CIP.  
Linear Leios crosses the breakeven threshold (~50 Tx kB/s assuming ~1400 B txs), while Praos does not. This means that Linear Leios not only improves scalability, but also sustainability in the medium term.

We’ve also invested significant effort comparing protocol variants and trade-offs, available [here](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1iH2LGHzXrF_r7_26OchL7GMSgmSu6J-nbHLZg-_u5iw/edit?usp=sharing).

If higher throughput is considered essential, it would be valuable to define *what specific performance target is required and why*, since higher throughput typically comes at the cost of:

- increased latency (due to additional protocol stages),
- more complex conflict resolution, or
- fragmented liquidity from UTxO sharding.


### Front- vs. Back-loading Ecosystem Costs

> “We should take the ecosystem compatibility issue seriously and let the ecosystem start getting ready as soon as possible…”

Absolutely - and that’s precisely the rationale for Linear Leios.

There’s an inherent trade-off between introducing a radically different sharded ledger early (with significant complexity and adoption overhead) versus delivering an incremental upgrade that achieves most of the performance benefits while keeping existing infrastructure compatible.

A sharded ledger - by design - requires the ecosystem to rethink liquidity management, and cross-shard dApp interactions.  
For example, multi-dApp transactions relying on shared UTxO liquidity would face major design challenges in a fully sharded environment.

Linear Leios, on the other hand:

- avoids UTxO fragmentation,  
- avoids transaction conflicts, and  
- keeps downstream applications compatible with minimal or no changes.

This approach allows the node, wallet, and dApp ecosystems to evolve and mature incrementally, rather than absorbing a massive protocol shift all at once.

Moreover, as @mpizenberg pointed out, this period of Linear Leios development coincides with significant tooling and node diversity improvements across languages - something the ecosystem urgently needs before tackling a more complex ledger.  
Without this maturity, deploying a highly concurrent, sharded system too early could easily outpace the readiness of both developers and tools, leading to slower adoption and fragmentation.

Finally, there’s an economic argument: scaling capacity prematurely does not guarantee demand.  
A high fixed-cost, high-throughput system without corresponding transaction volume can actually harm long-term sustainability.  
Linear Leios mitigates this risk by adapting throughput dynamically (through adaptive announcing, voting & certification of EBs) to current network demand.

### On dApp Composability and Transaction Conflicts

Building on @Quantumplation’s excellent [blog post](https://www.314pool.com/post/leios#transaction-conflict) and the follow-up discussion on Leios trade-offs:

The future of Cardano DeFi should not remain a collection of isolated dApps.  
The eUTxO model uniquely enables cross-dApp composition within a single transaction - a property we must preserve and encourage.

Attempting to completely eliminate UTxO contention or shard it away risks undermining this composability.

---
Linear Leios is not a detour - it’s a strategic building block.

In other words, Linear Leios is the pragmatic path:  
it gets us closer to the end goal by keeping the system live, sustainable, and evolvable - rather than risking multi-year stalls or premature complexity.

I don't think using a map would be appropriate as it won't preserve the order of the transactions in EBs which is essential for Cardano's ledger integrity.

cc @lehins

You are both correct! :smile: 

Having just sequence of transactions is incorrect, since then you could have different multiple entries in the list with duplicate hashes but different size. In such a case when it would be decoded in the implementation, with that implementation using a Map, then one of those entries would disappear. That would be bad, despite that by definition one of those entries would be invalid (since changing the size will change the hash). In other words it would allow for EB to have invalid entries in the serialization which would get ignored, which one exactly would get ignored would be implementation specific. We had occurrences of such incorrect definition in Ledger, which we have fixes since.

On the other hand, despite that using a map solves the problem with duplicates, it does not preserve order, which is also important.

The proper solution is to use an ordered map here. CDDL does not have an official definition like that, but we do already have in Ledger CDDL examples of ordered sets. In a similar fashion we can add definition of an ordered map. We do have support for such data structure in Haskell already and use it for some data in the ledger state.

In other words, I would suggest accepting the suggestion with added comment that this Map definition will use order preserving (de)serialization. From what I know CDDL does not say anything about the order or how duplicates are handled, so we can choose how we interpret this map definition.

# Front-Running in Linear Leios vs Ouroboros Praos

Opening this thread to directly address the recent community concern that Linear Leios is significantly more vulnerable to front-running/MEV than Praos, and that full/parallel Leios would largely solve the problem.

That claim is not correct.
Any protocol delivering 30-60× higher throughput will necessarily create proportionally more ordering-dependent value. That is not a flaw, it is the entire point.

Linear Leios actually has fewer front-running vectors than the full/parallel design (no decoupled IB stage, no separate EB production cadence).

Most importantly, the protocol has one extremely strong, built-in incentive that keeps ordering-sensitive transactions exactly as safe as they are in Praos today.

## The Incentive

If a slot leader puts a high-value ordering opportunity (a "V-tx") in an Endorser Block, the very next leader can skip the certificate with zero risk and steal the entire opportunity for themselves.

→ No rational slot leader will ever do that.
→ Certified EBs therefore contain almost exclusively non-sensitive bulk traffic (B-tx).
→ All ordering-sensitive traffic (large swaps, liquidations, oracle updates, competitive mints etc.) is automatically forced into RBs and retains exactly the same front-running resistance as Praos.

This works perfectly with Cardano’s batcher AMMs too - the batcher is the one who extracts value, so the incentive to keep valuable batches in RBs is unchanged.

## Complex / Plutus-heavy dApps

The incentive to skip still exists in theory, but is negligible in practice:

- Skipping only pays if the stolen value > total EB fees
→ expected to be extremely rare.
- Per-transaction Plutus budget is raised ~10× globally
→ most currently-tight scripts now fit in RBs.
- Truly heavy workloads are almost always non-sensitive (B-tx)
→ no reason to skip.
- Private submission to trusted SPOs remains available for guaranteed RB inclusion.

## Bottom line
Linear Leios does **not** weaken front-running resistance in any meaningful way. It cleanly separates sensitive and non-sensitive traffic by itself, using a very strong economic incentives, while giving the ecosystem vastly more capacity for everything else.

We would very much welcome concrete counter-examples - specific dApps, scripts, or realistic scenarios - that would actually be worse off under Linear Leios than under current Praos.

I've now watched the video twice, and I actually agree with @dcoutts and Neil's concern.

The core of the problem comes down to the fact that Linear Leios enables *instant gratification* for bad behavior while Full Leios does not. In Linear Leios, if a malicious SPO sees an EB with a profitable trade, it can:

1. Ignore the EB.
2. Create its own tx that takes advantage of the profitable trade (a replacement attack).
3. Add this new MEV tx into the Praos block *instead of* the EB certificate.
4. Profit as soon as the block is confirmed by the network.

With Full Leios, this *instant gratification* is not possible. If a malicious SPO sees an EB with a profitable trade, that SPO can't simply add their own version of that tx into the RB. Instead, they must add it to an IB and send it through the entire Leios pipeline for a future SPO to possibly place in an RB. **This is because in Full Leios, RBs can only hold EBs, not individual txs.**

The increased concern about front-running directly follows from this difference in design. Right now, an SPO can only see what is inside their mempool - about 200 kb. To find a profitable MEV opportunity, they only have 200 kbs of txs to look through. But with Linear Leios, the EB block gives them an extra 10 mb or more. That is 500x more information at their disposal. Odds of finding a profitable MEV opportunity sky-rocket and the instant gratification possible with Linear Leios make it possible to take advantage of any opportunities found in this extra 10 mb of txs.

Again, **in Full Leios, the SPO sees more data too but they can't take advantage of it due to the way txs actually get included in RBs**.

Two points come to mind:
- To protect a tx from being front-run in Cardano today, one must not forward such a tx to other block producers and include it directly in a block (or trust an SPO to that for you). The same front-running protection is available with the Linear Leios protocol. It will harm throughput, but the remaining throughput will be strictly higher than with Praos alone. Besides, the increased volume of activity to front run does not exist and can't exist with Praos alone because there is no demand without capacity (the premise of this CIP as identified by CPS-18).
- More a silver lining: With Linear Leios, front-running is easier to detect than today. That is, if a transaction is part of an EB, which gets certified and L_diff has passed, but an SPO does _not_ include the cert and instead chooses to forge a block that conflicts with the certified tx set, it's a strong indicator they deliberately did so. Still plausible deniable though, unless they also voted for the EB. I'm not implying an incentive scheme here, but just want to mention _detect-ability_.

Thank you guys for the comments. My two cents on this one:

> Right now, an SPO can only see what is inside their mempool - about 200 kb. …  Odds of finding a profitable MEV opportunity sky-rocket and the instant gratification possible with Linear Leios make it possible to take advantage of any opportunities found in this extra 10 mb of txs.

*TLDR*: Linear Leios maintains the same or a lower level of risk exposure of users to MEV attacks.


A rational/MEV-hunting SPO in Praos can easily observe a higher amount of traffic than 200 kb, e.g., by increasing the mempool limit, setting up multiple nodes in different parts of the network, etc. Hence, publicly available MEV opportunities will be known to rational nodes early on, and not after they appear in an RB. 

Further, these txs will most likely be exposed to a higher risk of being front-run in Praos. Given the limited throughput of Praos compared to Linear Leios, it will take longer for a tx of this type to be included in a block, and thus more block producers are going to consider it for inclusion. Hence, it is more likely that the tx is picked up by a rational block producer,that will try to extract value from it.

Finally, users can avoid publicizing their tx and getting exposed to MEV attacks in Linear Leios in the same way as in Praos: by coordinating with specific SPOs and having their txs being directly included in an RB. Note, that this service is naturally supported in Linear Leios, as for the parameters considered in the CIP, by design for a large fraction of RBs there will be no certified EB to be included due to the last RB being generated within the previous RB’s diffusion period, and instead the RB will directly contain txs.

> Which protocol specification is this referring to? ... To my understanding any of the Leios variants must allow RBs to directly hold txs or it would endanger safety (and by extension liveness) properties, for a certificate may never be produced given enough adversarial stake. So unfortunately your conclusion of "why this is a non-issue in Full Leios" doesn't hold.

@ch1bo [This](https://iohk.io/en/research/library/papers/ouroboros-leios-design-goals-and-concepts/) isn't a specification, but these are direct quotes:

> ... the ranking blocks form a traditional linear blockchain, but instead of containing transactions, they contain references to endorsement blocks ...
> -- Section 4.2.1

> Under extreme conditions when participation drops and the remaining active block producers represent too small a fraction of stake, ... [the protocol] evaluates a predicate on the recent chain which then determines if the protocol should be in ‘optimistic’ or ’pessimistic’ mode. ... In optimistic mode, things proceed as described previously. In pessimistic mode, the ranking block is created containing transactions directly, without any endorsement blocks.
> -- Section 4.3.6

The key distinction here is *who decides* what goes in the RB. Linear Leios leaves the choice up to the current slot leader while Full Leios has the protocol make and enforce the choice. (Although it didn't really go into detail about how the protocol decides.)

@pagio @berewt I think my comments are being misunderstood. **I am not trying to eliminate MEV** - that's not possible. **I am also not suggesting a change to Linear Leios**. I am trying to point out **a potential trust assumption** we can use instead of enforcing anything at the protocol level. Instead of evaluating this trust assumption, the discussion keeps going on tangents about MEV...

The core problem is that txs in an RB means there is no throughput boost for that block. As a crisis fallback or in the case of low demand, this is fine. But if txs are placed in RBs under non-crisis/high-demand periods, this is not good! The MEV prevention service that keeps being suggested is not good for this reason. If MEV happens inside an EB, that is fine because we still get the throughput boost for that block. But if MEV results in txs in RBs, that forces us to sacrifice significant throughput.

So the question I've been trying to point out is: _how do we prevent txs in RBs even in the presence of MEV?_ I think we can solve this with just a social contract. Below is the second half of my prior [comment](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/pull/1078#discussion_r2549920094) that seems to have been missed. **It does not need to be baked into Linear Leios!** If people just delegate away from SPOs who deviate from the norm, that is good enough.

> 1. For all stake pools, track their ratio of RBs with txs vs EB certificates over a given time-frame. Use this to generate a global average ratio.
> 2. If an SPO's individual average is ever meaningfully higher than this global average, either it has a technical issue or it is frequently using the RB to front-run. Either way, honest delegators should delegate away.
>
> If there is actually a systemic problem [or low systemic demand], the global average of the tx/EB ratio should rise. So as long as the majority of honest stake prefers throughput over [txs] in RBs, the global average should be near optimal. In this context, an SPO trying to [put txs in RBs] too frequently will cast an immediate spotlight on their bad behavior and they will lose delegators. 

Under this pressure, MEV can still happen inside EBs but that isn't as bad because it doesn't sacrifice significant throughput. As long as the community enforces this global ratio, the MEV prevention service that keeps being suggested can work similarly by using EBs instead of txs in RBs.

Again, **this doesn't require a change to Linear Leios**. It is a social contract, not a protocol enforced metric.

@pagio The attack you describe would not work in the system I am imagining. Consider an entirely off-chain **Mithril-based Availability Monitoring** system. Whenever an RB contains txs instead of an EB cert, a poll can go out to all SPOs: "Did you see an EB cert that met the `X%` stake threshold before it was time to produce that RB?" To declare the RB producer's action as malicious, the poll would need to achieve the *same stake threshold* as the EB certificate itself. So your scenario would fail because the poll would not meet the required threshold of "Yes".

Some important points about the monitoring system (as I see it):
- **It is purely off-chain.** It has no impact on consensus and requires no changes to the Linear Leios protocol.
- **It is for observation only.** It is just a community tool for logging and transparency.
- **Data can be pruned regularly**. The results are only needed for short-term accountability. We don't need it to replay the chain.

This mithril-based polling system may also be useful for observing other parts of the distributed system.

Something like this might work:
- Sum up all the available inputs to the transaction (inputs + positive mints)
- iterate through the certificates, in order
  - for each deposit, deduct it from the running balance
  - for each withdrawal, add it to the running balance
  - if at any point it goes negative, fail

This ensures that any assets involved in the transfers to and from accounts *exist*, and don't get created out of thin air. > If you try to impose a balancing order, some part of the transaction will always be screwed.

@lehins This doesn't seem to be true. At a high-level, a tx effectively *unlocks value **and then** re-locks it.* So there seems to be a clear order of operations here: add up all `sources` and then subtract off all `consumers`. IMHO the problem with @Quantumplation's example and your example is that `withdrawals` are not counted as *sources of value* when they fundamentally are sources to the tx. As long as withdrawals are always processed *before* deposits, I don't see any issues, even in nested txs.

If a tx tries to withdraw 100 ADA and then deposit 100 ADA, _it should fail if the account didn't have 100 ADA before the tx_. It doesn't matter that this tx is balanced; it should fail phase 1 validation. This is already how Cardano works: what is stopping me from withdrawing 100 ADA and creating a UTxO with that 100 ADA? The ledger currently rejects this tx if the account didn't have 100 ADA to begin with; it doesn't matter that this tx is balanced.

For nested txs, the same rule applies except each sub-tx is processed sequentially, followed by the top-level tx. Let's say we have an account with a starting balance of 100 ADA and then these sub-txs:

```
sub_tx_1 => deposits 100 ADA
sub_tx_2 => withdraws 100 ADA
sub_tx_3 => withdraws 100 ADA
```

Then these are some possible orders and there expected results:
```
[sub_tx_1, sub_tx_2, sub_tx_3] => Succeeds
[sub_tx_2, sub_tx_3, sub_tx_1] =>
    Fails because the account's balance is 0 ADA after processing sub_tx_2. There is nothing
    for sub_tx_3 to withdraw.
```

As long as withdrawals are always processed before deposits and nested txs processes sub-txs sequentially, I don't see any security risks here. It seems fine to allow first withdrawing from an account and then depositing back into it in the same tx.

> If we don't have this restriction then anyone can just create any token and then destroy it within the same transaction.

This does not seem to be true as long as we process withdrawals first. A tx can't withdraw a token that doesn't exist before the tx.

> As long as withdrawals are always processed before deposits, I don't see any issues, even in nested txs.

That is what I was saying to @Quantumplation and I'll just expand on it.
There is no order in which deposits, inputs, refunds withdrawals, etc. are validated in a transaction, when it comes to balancing out a transaction. In a `UTXO` Ledger rule we simply sum up all the produced amounts and ensure that value is equal to the amount that is consumed by the transaction. That's how it has always been.

If we start defining the order in which balancing of a transaction happens, it will be a fundamental change to the ledger logic that will create a lot of conflict, including for various DApps. If we start doing it only for direct_deposits/withdrawals then it will be a massive inconsistency with how we've always handled transaction balancing.

The state update happens in a specific order, which is why you are probably thinking that there is order to this validation. What a lot of people don't realize is that validation and state update are two completely separate things, when it comes to balancing a transaction. It is a case that state update within a transaction can affect the validation of other parts of a transaction (eg. that's why we first apply withdrawals before we validate and apply certificates), but not when it comes to balancing out the funds.

In other words: "If a tx tries to withdraw 100 ADA and then deposit 100 ADA" this is not how we should look at a transaction on Cardano. Maybe that's how people want to think about it, but that is not how it is or should be. In a Cardano transaction, as long as the net change in assets is equal to 0, the transaction is said to balance out, hence is valid.



> For nested txs, the same rule applies except each sub-tx is processed sequentially, followed by the top-level tx.

No, for nested transaction it especially breaks a lot of things! Here is an example (assume original balances in accounts a 0):
```
tx = 
  { ins = ...
  , outs = ...
  , fee = ...
  , subTransactions =
    [ subTx1 = 
      { inputs = ...
      , direct_deposits = [cred0 => BAR:200]
      , withdrawals = [cred1 => FOO:200]
      }
    , subTx2 = 
      { inputs = [BAR:200]
      , outputs = [FOO:200]
      , ...
      }
    ]
  }
```

How would you expect the direct deposit to succeed, if the actual BAR token is being supplied by a subsequent transaction? Why not swap subTx1 and subTx2? We can't, cause then withdrawal of FOO will happen after the output that requires FOO is created.

Fine, then maybe we allow inputs from subsequent outputs to balance out the direct deposits? Which is what the actual plan is for Nested Transactions, since that is were its real power comes from. However, here is where this idea really breaks:
```
tx =
  { ins = ...
  , outs = ...
  , fee = ...
  , subTransactions =
    [ subTx1 = 
      { inputs = ...
      , outputs = ...
      , direct_deposits = [cred0 => 2M ADA]
      }
    , subTx2 = 
      { inputs = [3M ADA]
      , outputs = [3M ADA]
      , withdrawals = [cred0 => 2M ADA]
      }
    ]
  }
```
All of the sudden it looks like there was a transfer of 5M ADA in one transaction, where in reality it was only 3M ADA and thus we minted 2M ADA within a transaction out of thin air.

To sum it up. If we start processing deposits/withdrawals in a specific order, it creates a dangerous incompatibility with the rest of the system. That is not the direction I would like to go in. It is much safer to disallow withdrawals and deposits into the same account for the same asset. Note, that operating on another asset for the same account doesn't creates a cause for concern.

```suggestion
[CIP-112 | Observe Script Type](https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/blob/master/CIP-0112/README.md) introduces Guards, which are arbitrary scripts that can be required by the transaction builder. It seems natural to tap into this functionality to allow sub-transaction builders to require arbitrary scripts to be executed at the top-level as well. In order to achieve that, sub-transactions will have a new field `requiredTopLevelGuards`, which will not be available in the top level transaction. The only enforcement that Ledger will have to do is to make sure that script hashes listed in that field are also present in the list of Guards in the top-level transaction. It will be the responsibility of the top level transaction builder to satisfy this requirement by adding all of the required guards from sub-transactions in the top level transaction. Moreover, in case when required guard is a plutus script, top level transaction builder will have to supply the redeemer for that script.
```

I don't like this. It breaks a critical invariant that is currently preserved by all multi-asset values, namely that quantity must always be non-zero. It is common in smart contract logic when you want to check if a value contains some token or not to simply check for the presence of the policy id (if your contract knows the policy id only supports a single token name, or to check for a policy id and asset name otherwise, no need to check that the quantity is greater than zero in an output because that is an invariant that is guaranteed by the ledger and value operations. 

This will be particularly important when changing the type of `txInfoWdrl` to `Map Credential AccountValue`. We must ensure that `AccountValue` has no zero quantity entries otherwise we undermine the entire value proposition of `BuiltinValue` which is to produce a single canonical representation of multi-asset value that preserves the invariants that all multi-asset values possess in the ledger. 
There must be a better way to handle this, for instance, we separate the whitelisted zero quantity tokens into their own list:

```haskell
data AccountState era
  = AccountState
  { balance :: !(CompactForm (AccountValue era))
  -- ^ Current multi-asset balance of the account.
  , whitelist :: !(CompactForm (ZeroQuantityWhitelisted era)

  type ZeroQuantityWhitelisted C.DijkstraEra = StrictMap C.PolicyId C.AssetName
  ```

An `AccountBalance` for an account is the unique map `Map PolicyID (Map AssetName Quantity)` such that, when encoded into a canonical Merkle trie, it yields `accountValueRoot`.
The domain of this map corresponds to the account’s whitelist. Normal direct deposits and withdrawals may only change the `Quantity` values of existing entries; only `stake_credential_adjust_whitelist` certificates may add or remove `(PolicyID, AssetName)` keys from the `AccountBalance`’s domain.
The ledger implementation maintains the underlying trie structure in its node storage; only `accountBalanceRoot` is stored in the canonical ledger state.

The ADA component of the account’s Value (as commit to by the `accountBalanceRoot`) must equal `coinBalance` (or vice versa) and enforce an invariant that they match.

```
accountValue :: AccountState era -> AccountBalance
accountValue as =
  case accountValueRoot as of
    Nothing -> mempty
    Just r  -> decodeAccountBalance r  -- "the unique map committed by r"
applyDeposit     :: AccountBalance -> AccountValueDelta -> AccountBalance
applyWithdrawal  :: AccountBalance -> AccountValueDelta -> Either Error AccountBalance

--After all applications we recommit:
encodeAccountValue :: AccountValue -> AccountValueRootHash

newRoot = encodeAccountValue newAccountValue
```
So spec-wise, the story is:
1. Take accountValueRoot from AccountState.
2. Conceptually decode to a logical map.
3. Apply deposit/withdrawal rules on that map.
4. Encode it back to a new root and store that as accountValueRoot'.

Under the hood, a full node will not materialize a giant map for every account on every tx. Instead, it maintains an indexed store of trie nodes keyed by their hashes:
Somewhere in node DB:
```
db[hash] = encoded_trie_node
```
In the ledger implementation:
```haskell
lookupAsset :: AccountValueRootHash -> (PolicyID, AssetName) -> Quantity
lookupAssets :: AccountValueRootHash -> [AssetId] -> AccountBalance
updateAssets :: AccountValueRootHash -> AccountValueDelta -> Either Error AccountValueRootHash
```
These functions are implemented using trie traversal / updates + node DB.

For a pure Haskell ledger library, you might model the DB as an extra parameter or an abstract interface; for the actual node, it’s wired into the node’s storage layer. The node is responsible for performing the relevant lookups / updates for these functions.

There are two approaches from here, the first is to not require the merkle proofs for these operations to be included in txs in which case:
- Full nodes trust their own DB.
- The root is a commitment for future or for light clients.
- This is closest to what we have today just more compact and more scalable internally.
The second approach requires merkle proofs for these operations to be included in the transactions, this increases offchain complexity in exchange for massive gains in tx validation performance and allowing light clients and stateless nodes to validate without having the full trie DB. 

The first approach is already a huge improvement on what we have now so there is no need to overcomplicate and introduce stateless validation now when it's not a bottleneck yet. We can proceed with root is stored on-ledger; full nodes maintain tries off-ledger; ledger rules use helper functions that read/update the tries using the root as an index.
In this case, what a full node would do is:

- Has a DB: db[hash] = encodedTrieNode.
- For each (asset, delta) in the tx:
  - Compute the key for the trie (e.g. k = hash(policy || assetName)).
  - Walk the trie from root to the leaf for k, loading only nodes on that path:
  - If leaf exists → oldQty.
  - If not → treat oldQty = 0 (but maybe not whitelisted).
  - Check whitelist semantics + interval constraints.
  - Compute newQty = oldQty + delta, fail if negative.
  - Rebuild nodes along that path with newQty, hash upwards → new root.
- Do that for each updated asset; the code can batch them so it doesn’t re-walk shared prefixes unnecessarily.
From the ledger’s perspective, this is exactly what `applyDeposit` / `applyWithdrawal` but implemented as `updateAccountBalance root deltas`.


must be replaced with:
```haskell

```
Along with a new field added to the transaction body, `requiredBalanceIntervals` which has the type `unordered_set<(stake_credential, policy_id, asset_name)>`. The script context `txInfoRequiredBalanceIntervals` will only contain the balance intervals for the entries in the account balance that are in the `requiredBalanceIntervals` field of the transaction body.   -> Either Error AccountBalanceCommitment

```suggestion
The rule of thumb is that when we calculate a hash of the data we take into account only the live (non deleted) values in canonical order. In the case when there is a single dump without delta records, this is exactly the order of how values are stored. But when delta—records appear we need to take into account that in the following records there may be values that are smaller than the ones in the base and some values may be deleted or updated. As a result writer should calculate a live-set of values, which can be done by running a streaming multi-merge algorithm (when we search for a minimal value from multiple records). In the case a value exists in multiple records we use a last—writer—wins rule. If there is a tombstone, we consider a value deleted and do not include it in a live-set.
```

There are a couple points here that I do not agree with:
* Simplicity. First and for most, it is not the submitting user that supplies the `isValid` flag, but the node that builds the block is the entity that sets this flag. Because of this `isValid` is not even part of the binary format of a transaction any more (see #1089). So, I totally agree with @teodanciu, it would be useful to have the same binary representation for transaction submission protocol as well as its representation in the block, since that approach results in the most overall simplicity
* Compactness:
  * I don't think using run length encoding would be the most compact way to represent this information in a block. Most importantly, I think such micro-optimization would introduce a totally unnecessary complexity and easy source of dangerous bugs. Moreover, as @teodanciu already pointed out, savings would be negligible if present at all, since 99.9% of transactions have `isValid = True`, which means for most blocks it is just an empty array. If anything a bit vector would be even more efficient way to represent this, since most of the time it would be just 0, but even that is not worth the complexity, despite having simpler and more efficient runtime and memory implementation.
  * Not that it is relevant, but just to have our facts straight this is not quite accurate "using an array of 16bit indices". It is not accurate because CBOR does not encode integral values in fixed width, so the overhead of each integral element in a CBOR array could be 1 byte for small values, even if the maximum accepted size is much higher like 64bits or even infinite.


> How much inefficiency is acceptable at the cost of simplicity?

I can measure inefficiency. It is only if you give me a metric on simplicity and its mathematical relationship to inefficiency that I will be able to answer that question :wink:

One small suggestion for emphasis (not scope expansion): it could be helpful to explicitly mention that script-level post-quantum capabilities are one part of a broader, longer-term effort toward making the whole Cardano stack post-quantum ready. From my understanding, similar considerations apply to Plutus scripts in terms of execution units and resource usage. This makes builtin support especially valuable, since hand-rolled implementations would likely be much more expensive.

I really like how this section already highlights that different post-quantum schemes come with different trade-offs. One optional way to strengthen this section could be to group those trade-offs a bit more explicitly from a developer or engineering perspective.

For example, some factors that may matter differently depending on the use case could include:
- signature size (impact on transaction size and data handling),
- verification key size (wallet and storage considerations),
- signature verification cost (script execution resources),
- diversity of cryptographic assumptions (to hedge against future breakthroughs).

This kind of framing might help make it clearer why there may not be a single “best” scheme, and why different applications might reasonably prefer different trade-offs.

As an optional clarification, we can mention a few well-known post-quantum signature families or schemes purely as illustrative examples, without implying any preference or decision. For instance, some schemes are often described as more “balanced,” others as having more compact signatures, and others as being more conservative but larger.

Even a high-level mention like this could help readers who are less familiar with the post-quantum landscape better understand what kinds of trade-offs the open questions are referring to.

It could be very valuable to provide supporting materials such as simple guidance, example usage patterns, and possibly benchmarking results showing relative verification costs. This would help developers make informed choices without needing deep cryptography expertise.

IMO; we need a CPS that covers and indexes all attack surfaces for when a QC hits the scene, so I do not think it is _just_ a plutus problem. As an overview

- For Praos we have a KES key, which under the hood uses a tree of keys on the ed25519 curve
- The cold key that ultimately binds a stake pool also uses keys from the ed25519 curve.
- The VRF that we use for Praos leadership selection is also using the ed25519 curve
- Then we have in plutus various built-ins that use curves that will break (ecds/schnorr over Secp256k1, and bls pairing crypto).
- the security of our hash functions will also be halved (Grover's algorithm), so we would need to go from sha256 -> sha512 for example, in all places (probably the easiest fix, though block/tx hashes will get bigger)

As you can see, if we get a quantum computer, our consensus and settlement layer will probably be attacked first, so the problem is wider.

But from this overview we also see what kind of quantum tools and construction we will need (not only signature schemes);  we will also need a VRF, KES construction, and most likely some quantum secure ZK scheme. 

A complex problem with many open questions. And from a presentation that @hjeljeli32 gave once, I think the best we can do now, is redesign our code base that we can swap in and out our underlying crypto primitives (which is also probably not trivial). This way, we can adapt ourselves to new schemes that pop up, but research needs to drive this solution space.

Given this broader context, another open question is; given that QC has broken the above schemes, how can we ensure that bootstrapping nodes follow the right chain?

E.g, QC breaks the forward security of the KES keys that sign blocks

I don't follow the argument of re-using inlined data.

If a transaction wants to spend an output that carries inlined data, that data would already be in the utxo set and thus the creating tx paid for it. For "normal" datum use, there would only be a datumhash on the utxo and the spending transaction provides the preimage in the witness set. This data resolves across any spent inputs that are parameterized by the same data (hash). I don't know how this evolves for nested transactions but I would expect it to allow re-use of hashed data. For other validation purposes, there is no datum in the context.

So, what exactly motivates the sketched change of `getDatum` in the agda spec?

I doubt that this will make anything easier at the point of validating transactions within a node because it will be presented with a completely ordered batch and just needs to validate it.

Any code that assembles nested transactions must be aware of the UTxO graph and how (sub-)transactions are to be balanced using inputs/outputs and correctly sequence them for these reasons.

In fact, to "enable more flexible script sharing within the batch" the (nested) transaction creating code would not use reference scripts at all and instead use script hashes and include the script once in the witness set. So maybe you meant here to improve script sharing _across_ batches?

Comparing to just including the witness set, adding a script to the UTxO will require the user to lock up the funds in the form of minUtxO, so that is the motivating factor against it. Which means the only reason why a user would want to do this instead of just using a script in witnesses is for further reuse.

So, this statement is incorrect: "not require the additional deposit for the reference script" There is still deposit for including a script in the output.

https://github.com/cardano-foundation/CIPs/blob/master/CPS-0021/CPD/README.md#2-the-grinding-attack-algorithm

So the attack arises when the adversary can corrupt the parties covering the last $x$ blocks before the evolving nonce is frozen to become the next epoch nonce. Each nonce contribution is deterministic and offers no choices, but the adversary can choose to create or not create each of the $x$ blocks. This gives rise to $2^x$ choices for the next epoch nonce.

The ability to execute this attack relies on the power of the adversary to select which parties they want to corrupt at will -- having seen the state of the protocol -- but with the "hey no fair!" constraint that they are not allowed to corrupt 50% or more of the stake. This is a very strong power, indeed arguably it's a ridiculously strong power, but it is helpful because showing protocols are still resistant in the face of a strong adversary is a better result than with a weaker adversary. And then Praos is resistant to this attack because an adaptive adversary can't know which parties to corrupt to control the last $x$ blocks. This effectively reduces the adversary's advantage back to that of a static adversary.

And the concern here is that with a public leader schedule, an adaptive adversary _can_ know exactly which parties to corrupt to control the last $x$ blocks, without any danger of them exceeding the "hey no cheating!" limit of 50%.

And the conclusion of this is that at best, one may want to analyse this in the context of a static rather than adaptive adversary.

@perturbing Does this sound right to you?

I have to say, the more I think about the adaptive adversary model the more I think it's unrealistic. I accept it's a helpful and tractable model for analysis, and making the adversary more powerful gives better theoretical results. But it's frankly bonkers to say that an attacker is so powerful that they can corrupt whomever they like whenever they like, but that they're not so powerful that they can just keep doing that and corrupt 50% or more of the stake. The "no more than 50%" constraint is supposed to correspond to the reality that corrupting parties is actually hard. In reality, an attacker will try to corrupt as many parties as they can, targeting those with weaker defences and those with more stake. And they will try to corrupt parties silently over a period of time and then wait. They're not going to choose on the basis of who has which particular slots (just those that have more slots).
Oh, and obviously anti-grinding measures (as recently proposed) would be very helpful.

> I disagree here; we see this kind of behavior with MEV; big pools get paid to order in a certain way.

Asking a pool to reorder transactions is not a full corruption under the adaptive adversary model. It's some partial thing that I don't think the model accounts for.

Are you arguing that pools will be bribed to include or exclude a block as part of a grinding attack? It's somewhat plausible to imagine asking them to definitely not create a block to allow an adversary who already has quite a bit of stake under their control to have a longer run of blocks with which to grind. But I don't think it's plausible to imagine actually including other not-fully-corrupted parties into a grinding attack unwittingly: the level of coordination would be too high. The "unwitting" victim would need to share the nonce output and then configure their system to receive and act on an automated instruction to either create or not create their block. Basically honest parties that are prepared to reorder transactions are not going to do something like that. It would clearly be crossing a line into dishonest behaviour.

> And this relates to my remark about whether we should add something to a code base that models a different (stronger) security model, as it gives a false sense of security (not a good practice).

It is worth noting that the _existing_ reference implementation of Cardano includes code for several different protocols, with different security models:

 * PBFT -- "permissive" BFT: a transitional protocol used during the Byron reboot. The early part of the mainnet chain is validated using this protocol's validity rules.
 * TPraos -- "transitional" Praos: a transitional protocol used during the Shelley era while SPOs were still coming online. It combined a BFT round robin schedule for "core" block producers with a Praos private slot leader schedule, with a parameter to control the fraction of blocks from each. Thus this had a partially public / partially private slot leader schedule. This was also therefore not secure against an adaptive adversary that corrupts the old core block producers.
 * Praos
 * OBFT -- Ouroboros BFT, but actually just a cut-down simplified version, not the one from the paper. It just uses the Ouroboros longest chain rule in combination with a round robin schedule. Obviously this is only intended for use against a 30% adversary.

The first three of these are used on mainnet (for current or historical parts of the chain). Anyone can use them in the older era in test nets or partner chains. Hopefully they are aware of the security trade-offs! I don't think we make this as clear as we could do.

> IMO, following the Unix philosophy, cardano-node should focus on one thing and do that really well: securing the Cardano mainnet. We have a great history of taking security seriously and being the slow but methodical chain; let's not throw that overboard.

Obviously we've always taken security seriously, but with accommodations and compromises to practicality and resource constraints (see for example the ongoing saga with the lack of proper KES). I would say we don't follow a Unix philosophy of do a single thing, but rather we always tried to make the code modular. This allows multiple protocols, multiple ledgers. And we have taken advantage of that flexibility, even on mainnet by having several variations over the years. We also originally designed the code with non-mainnet applications in mind. We demoed a "pokemon" ledger, and as noted above the code includes a BFT demo protocol. This has been carried in the codebase for _years_ without significant maintenance cost (because the code is structured in a modular way).

Hi everyone, I saw you started talking a bit more about grinding so I thought that I could give my opinion there. :) 

Regardless of whether the adaptive security model is realistic or not, and even without relying on this model, we demonstrated in the CIP with @nhenin that grinding attacks are possible. We did so without full knowledge of what the adversary can and want to do (can they DDOS, corrupt... ?), only with some probabilistic analysis.

The 50% limit is simply a limit/hypothesis chosen to prove when you have security. It does not mean there is a "hey no fair" rule in practice of course, simply that theoretically we do not know how much and cannot guarantee security  when an adversarsy has more, and so restrain the security argument to that case. You have to put a limit somewhere if you want to argue about security and come up with an efficient protocol, that is pretty much all that there is to it.
For grinding more specifically, you can grind with much less stake than that. The chances of having a "natural", "passive" grinding attacks become superlinear after 20% or 30% stake iirc. But there are "active" ways to increase your attack chances  (by snowballing over several epochs, not considering consecutive last blocks but simple majority over a period if you fork, etc.). 

Public elections are inherently more risky in blockchains as you have more information. If you think with the adaptive security model in mind, the adversary does not have to corrupt someone at random but can target it directly. That is much easier and effective, but still might not sound really realistic.
For grinding attacks more specifically, we do not need something as strong as corruption though. Simply DDOSing enough block producers, or preventing block transmission for example, to get a a high enough majority of blocks at the end of an epoch is sufficient.
To stress it again, we technically do not need to own the last consecutive blocks at the end of the epoch for a grinding attack, a majority of block at the end is sufficient. Knowing who are the block producers, the adversary can increase their majority efficiently and have their blocks be the de facto blocks ones (for instance by DDOSing block producers or preventing block transmission).

The CIP text currently says

> Note that this is a global or static protocol parameter, not a dynamic one that can be updated by on-chain governance. Making it a dynamic protocol parameter may be desirable in future: it would allow changing the algorithm after the chain has already been started. Like all dynamic protocol parameters, it could be changed by a governance action, with the effect taking place at an epoch boundary. Introducing a new dynamic protocol parameter would require a hard fork however.

The existing ledger spec has a load of "global" or "constant" parameters. The meaning of this new parameter should be understood in the context of the other such parameters in the existing ledger spec. In practice these are all set in the genesis file(s). Many previous hard forks introduce new global parameters which are then specified in the genesis file for that new era (after the hard fork).

That is, this CIP as written only allows for setting the global parameter in a genesis file. This could therefore be set in the genesis file of some future hard fork. The fact that the CIP allows for an unspecified value defaulting to Praos also enables implementations that want to to set the parameter in the genesis file of the current era. Obviously that only helps new chains, since existing chains cannot change their era genesis files.

The comment in the CIP there also says that plausibly there would be useful use cases where it would be useful to make it a dynamic protocol parameter. In which case having a feature flag e.g. in the local node's config files might be a way to go (like the way we enable experimental network protocol features for example).

It does not need to be, but an implementation can do that as an optimisation and still be faithful to the specification. As always, the ledger spec is a specification not an implementation. Any observably equivalent implementation is ok. Avoiding computing things that will never be used is therefore ok.

The key point here is to reassure everyone that no hard fork on mainnet is needed, even for node implementations that are (or could be) used on mainnet that choose to implement this CIP.

As written the only way to use the protocol is by setting it in an era's genesis file. That can take place at a hard fork that introduces the era.

I didn't spell it out in detail (and it's probably not worth spelling out in detail in this CIP) but my reasoning for saying that Linear Leios may result in a higher transaction latency than a pure Tachys deployment goes like this...

Assume that Linear Leios has the same basic latency from when a transaction makes it into the mempool to making it into the first block. Ok, you say sims show it might be slightly lower, so we'll keep that in mind.

Consider how a Linear Leios + Tachys vs a pure Tachys network would be tuned. Linear Leios takes advantages of the big gaps between blocks to put in these jumbo additional blocks. This is great for throughhput and roughly neutral for latency (perhaps some slight reduction). If (and indeed when) there are no such big gaps then the jumbo extra block cannot be included. In a pure Tachys network, the gaps between blocks in the Praos schedule are instead used for more (normal sized) blocks. So basically, a Linear Leios configuration will have higher throughput by having fewer but much bigger blocks, while a Tachys configuration will simply have more frequent but normal sized blocks. The more frequent blocks leads to a lower latency of finality (if not to lower latency of time to first block), at least for a throughput that each configuration can sustain. If a wallet needs to wait 10 blocks to reach its confidence threshold then that simply takes less wall clock time if blocks are produced more frequently.

Perhaps I should adjust the text to say something along these lines without going into full detail. Something like:

> One can expect a throughput vs finality latency trade-off: a Linear Leios configuration with big blocks should be able to achieve higher throughput, while a Tachys configuration configuration with more frequent but smaller blocks should be able to achieve a shorter time to reach a block depth that gives sufficient confidence in finality. Thus for some partner chain use cases that prioritise latency of finality over throughput, it may be preferable to disable Linear Leios.
